chapters.summary: First Deputy Commissioner Jeffrey Shear introduces agency representatives and explains the SCRIE and DRIE programs, detailing how DOF establishes frozen rent with property tax credits for owners, and reports 67,677 households served in 2024 including 50,071 DOF-SCRIE, 6,594 HPD-SCRIE, and 11,012 DRIE households.
chapters.title: DOF testimony on Rent Freeze program overview and statistics

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, we do have testimony.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Lee, Chair Zhuang, Chair Hanif, members of the Committees on Finance, Aging, and Disabilities, and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: My name is Jeffrey Shear, and I am the first Deputy Commissioner of the New York City Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on legislation affecting the rent freeze program, the senior citizen homeowners exemption, and the disability disabled homeowners exemption.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Joining me today to help answer questions after the testimony are Ryan Murray, Executive Deputy Commissioner and Chief Program Officer at the Department of Aging,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Alika Amprey-Samuels, Deputy Commissioner at Housing Preservation and Development,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Nisha Agarwal, Commissioner of the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, and Julie Walpert, Assistant Commissioner at Housing Preservation and Development.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Taken together, the proposals before the Council address an important policy question.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: How the city can make tax and rent relief more accessible for older New Yorkers and people with disabilities while ensuring

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: that the programs can be administered effectively.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I will begin with the Rent Freeze program.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The Rent Freeze program consists of two benefits, the Senior Citizen Rent Increase Exemption, or SCRI, and the Disability Rent Increase Exemption, or DRI.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Share the goal of helping older New Yorkers and people with disabilities remain in their homes by protecting them from future rent increases.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For eligible tenants,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF establishes a frozen rent amount.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: As the authorized regulated rent increases, the tenant generally continues to pay the frozen amount and the property owner receives a corresponding property tax credit for the difference.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Bless you.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The Rent Freeze program serves a substantial population.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In calendar year 2024, 67,677 New York City households received benefits.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That included 50,000

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In 71, DOF-administered SCRI households, 6,594 HPD-administered SCRI households in Mitchell-Lama housing, and 11,012 DRI households.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Participation increased steadily during much of the last decade before declining during the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In 2024, enrollment increased by 0.8%, the first annual increase since 2019.

chapters.summary: Shear describes DOF's outreach through senior center events, rent freeze clinics with elected officials, PEU's Benefits on Your Block initiative, targeted outreach to non-renewing participants, online application and renewal options, and a streamlined single application replacing separate initial and renewal forms.
chapters.title: DOF testimony on outreach and administrative improvements

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Expanding awareness has been an important part of DOF's work.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF's outreach unit and Rent Free's ombudspersons participate in information and enrollment events at senior centers, Rent Free's clinics hosted by council members and state legislators,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: and outreach and training sessions with community-based organizations, legal service providers, and social service organizations.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have also worked with other city agencies to improve awareness of the program and to provide application assistance.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have worked particularly closely with the Mayor's Public Engagement Unit.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Through PEU's Benefits on Your Block initiative, City staff provide eligibility screenings and enrollment assistance in communities across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF also provides PEU with information on rent-free participants who have failed to renew on time so that the city can conduct targeted outreach.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have also sought to reduce administrative barriers.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Applicants can now apply and renew entirely online, and DOF has replaced separate initial and renewal applications with a single streamlined application for most participants.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We continue to review and improve rent-freeze forms, notices, and other materials.

chapters.summary: Shear expresses DOF support for Intro 978A implementing the state's income ceiling increase to $75,000, projecting approximately 5,000 additional households and estimating fiscal impacts of $4.5 million in year one, $8.6 million in year two, and $13 million in year three.
chapters.title: DOF testimony supporting Intro 978A income limit increase

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF supports Intro 978A, which would implement legislative changes enacted by the state legislature to increase the rent-freeze program's income ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The recently enacted state budget authorizes New York City to increase the maximum income level for SCRI and DRI to $75,000 beginning July 1, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Intro 978A would make the corresponding change to the New York City Administrative Code retroactive to that date.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The increase would recognize that households with income above $50,000 can still face significant rent burdens in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Over time, nominal increases in Social Security, pension income, or wages may have pushed a household outside of the eligibility limits,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: even when the household's actual economic circumstances have not

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: materially improved.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF projects that the higher ceiling would increase enrollment by approximately 9% or about 5,000 households across SCRI and DRI.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The estimated fiscal impact is $4.5 million in the first year, $8.6 million in the second year, and $13 million in the third year.

chapters.summary: Shear notes DOF supports the objective of reducing administrative barriers but explains that the DOF-HPD division involves different workflows and payment mechanisms, requiring substantial technical upgrades, and welcomes working with the Council and HPD on implementation.
chapters.title: DOF testimony on Intro 307 universal application position

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: With regard to Introduction 307, which would require the Department of Finance and the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to create

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: universal initial and recertification applications for SCRI and for DRI,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF supports the objective of reducing administrative barriers and making it easier for tenants to apply for benefits.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: However, the current division of responsibilities between DOF and HPD is not simply a matter of two agencies using different forms.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: A universal form and online system for all households, regardless of type of residence, would require substantial technical and operational upgrades

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: and coordination between both agencies with different workflows and payment mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We welcome the opportunity to work with the Council and HPD on ways to achieve the bill's underlying goal while ensuring that

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: any new process can be implemented reliably and without creating new delays for applicants.

chapters.summary: Shear describes the Senior Citizens Homeowners Exemption and Disabled Homeowners Exemption programs, reporting 50,912 SCHE exemptions with $190.9 million tax expenditure and 2,500 DHE exemptions with $8.5 million expenditure in fiscal year 2026.
chapters.title: DOF testimony on SCHE and DHE homeowner exemption programs

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Two other introductions before the Council concern homeowner exemptions rather than rent-free program benefits, but they serve a closely related purpose,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: helping older homeowners and homeowners with disabilities to remain in their homes by reducing their property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The Senior Citizens Homeowners Exemption, or SHE, provides a partial reduction of a home's assessed value to qualifying senior homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The Disabled Homeowners Exemption, or DEHE, provides similar benefits

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: to qualifying homeowners with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: These are significant programs.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, DOF granted 50,912 SHE exemptions with $1.1 billion in exempt excess

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: value and an estimated tax expenditure of $190.9 million.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF also granted 2,500 Dehee exemptions in fiscal year 2026 with an estimated tax expenditure of $8.5 million.

chapters.summary: Shear discusses Intros 1010 and 934 on increasing SCHE benefits and income caps, noting DOF support but deferring positions pending budget clarity for fiscal year 2028, and addresses Intro 1033 on discretionary notice requirements and pre-considered 2458 on annual training, questioning whether mandating annual training is necessary given existing practice.
chapters.title: DOF testimony on Intros 1010, 934, 1033, and pre-considered 2458

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Introductions 1010 and 934 both would increase SHE benefits based on recently granted state authority.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Intro 1010, which relies on authority that was enacted as part of the state budget, increases the maximum SHE exemption for lower income senior homeowners from 50%

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: to 65% starting in fiscal year 2028, as well as increasing the income cap to $83,400.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Intro 934 relies on state authority that was enacted separate from the state budget at the end of the legislative session.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It would move up the start of increasing she benefits from 50% to 65% of property taxes owed to fiscal year 2027.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF is generally supportive of increasing the income cap and benefits for she.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: However, at this time, the city's budget has only funded increasing the income cap for she.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF therefore would like to defer our position on Intro 934 and on the benefit level increase in Intro 1010 until budget conditions become clearer for fiscal year 2028.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the Council on each of these bills.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Regarding Intro 1033, we need time to review the bill and how it would facilitate our communication with customers.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Regarding pre-considered 2458, DOF already provides training to other outreach staff from other agencies and will continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: As such, we don't know if making this an annual requirement is necessary.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I and my colleagues would be happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Anyone else have statement?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang questions Ryan Murray of DFTA on how the agency identifies and refers SCRIE-eligible older adults, with Murray reporting 1,752 individuals enrolled through older adult centers and 2,340 through case management programs, and describing outreach through town halls and PEU enrollment days.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks DFTA about SCRIE referral process and numbers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Now we're going to do the question part.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So I have my first, I will ask a question and then I will turn to the other chairs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The first question, how does DFTA and the NYC agent participate in identification and the referral process?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Screen eligible older adults, how many referrals did DFTA, Older Adult Center, case managers, and associate staff make in last year?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Chairs, Ryan Murray from the Department for the Aging.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And so we obviously defer to on eligibility and targeting to DOF.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: However, as you know, given our infrastructure, where we are citywide with our 308 older adult centers, and we have our case management programs,

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: our education, outreach, case assistance, and case management services allow us to make sure that folks have the most up-to-date information on SCREET, and we make those referrals.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So what we can tell you is we have over 1,752 individuals in our OSC network who

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: have SCREET as of last year, that's fiscal year, and over 2,340 individuals who are enrolled in SCREET through our case management program.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: What we've done with Department of Finance is host, as you've heard from the first deputy commissioner, whether it was targeted outreach at our older adult centers, we've had town halls.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: We have also worked with the Mears Public Engagement Unit to be present in community and have enrollment days at our centers and continue to disseminate information.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks about language services at centers, and Murray explains centers are required to provide culturally and linguistically relevant services with staff speaking community languages including Spanish and Chinese.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about language access and culturally relevant outreach

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So what's the language you provide?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have information?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So at our centers, as you know, we require that there is not just language, but cultural relevance in our case management programs as well.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: The individuals who are there speak the languages of the community.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So whether it's in English or they're working in multiple languages, Spanish, Chinese, and so on, that is a requirement for those programs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sorry, if they don't come to the center, how did you guys do the outreach?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Again, so our team will disseminate information to our older adult center teams, whether it's we have monthly meetings with our directors in the program so that those are relevant.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And if folks are part of the center or they're part of our case management program, that is where we make sure we are providing the hands-on support to complete those applications.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether DFTA reaches out to the deaf community like Mr. So's organization, and Murray acknowledges more can be done and welcomes the opportunity to work with the organization.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about outreach to deaf community

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Did you guys reach out to the deaf community, like Mr.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Soule's community?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: I think there's always much more that we can do, but our outreach channels are multiple.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: I would welcome the opportunity to work with the organization.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many staff are dedicated to SCRIE outreach, and Murray explains there is no dedicated SCRIE staff but at least 308 case assistance individuals across centers and 21+ case management programs provide benefit information and application help.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about dedicated SCRIE outreach staff

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can you please describe your current outreach process and the program in detail?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many staff are dedicated to assist in screen outreach and create information materials and help other adults through the application process?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: We don't have a dedicated number of staff to SCRI specifically.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: At our older adult centers, as you know, we have our case assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So each of the 308 centers has an individual or multiple individuals who provide case assistance across a range of benefits and services.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So the number is at least 308 individuals providing those services in our case management programs.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: There are multiple case managers.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: We have 21 programs citywide, so at least 21 or more individuals in those programs are dedicated to providing information.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And again, we partner when we think of outreach with our colleagues here at the Department of Finance who would be on the ground and with other parts of our city government.

chapters.summary: Zhuang presses on whether DFTA has outreach methods beyond senior centers, and Murray describes case management agencies serving over 30,000 homebound individuals, social media channels, and the Aging Connect call line for referrals.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about outreach beyond senior centers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So except the home senior centers, you don't have the other way to outreach so far, right?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: We serve through our case management agencies, which serves over 30,000 homebound individuals.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: That would be the channel where we're reaching folks who are not coming into the centers.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: In addition, we also feature information online.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Since the start of the admin, we've added over 5,000 followers to our social media.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: You're probably very familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So we use a range of channels to make sure we're outreaching.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And in terms of incoming, our Aging Connect program also provides referrals and assistance to individuals who are coming to us by calls.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Which social media?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Whether it's Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, those are our current channels.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether DFTA uses culturally sensitive platforms like WeChat or KakaoTalk, notes she has never seen SCRIE outreach on WeChat despite being active there, and urges outreach through ethnic newspapers and language-specific platforms to reach seniors who don't use Facebook or Instagram.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about culturally specific platforms like WeChat

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have culturally sensitive channels?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like people speak different language, they are in different platforms.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Did you guys do outreach there?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like say KK Talk for Korean community.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And we each have...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Chinese community?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: As you know, our partners on the ground, whether it's we saw each other recently at Homecrest for our programs, our providers are using those platforms actively.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Oh, I haven't seen any.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I am very active in WeChat, but I haven't seen any.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Just let you know.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And a lot of people, if they were in an environment to only speak certain languages, they're not going to go to Facebook or Instagram.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They even don't know what Facebook or Instagram is.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So I hope you guys can really do outreach for different ethnic community, different language platform, and really, like say, Jewish community, a lot of times they only read their newspaper.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So there's different people have different needs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Hopefully you guys really reach to those communities.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I see you guys have great translation in Chinese in Facebook, but not in WeChat.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But the Chinese speaking only seniors, they are only in WeChat, but there's no advertising there at all.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Just let you know.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks about the percentage of successful enrollments from DFTA referrals and whether DFTA uses a hotline, with Murray confirming enrolled numbers represent successful enrollments and that Aging Connect receives housing and benefits calls as top categories.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about enrollment success rate and hotline outreach

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And what's the percentage of FTA referral application successfully complete enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So again, the number that I gave you is the folks who are currently enrolled in the SCRE program.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So those are successful enrollments in the program.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Does DFTA use a hotline or general outreach to promote SCRE energy?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Yes, individuals that come to us via our Aging Connect program, one of our top calls is consistently housing

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: and benefits is also one of our top calls and that is where we provide that assistance.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how DFTA ensures seniors without internet or technology skills aren't left behind, and how homebound seniors are reached, with Murray explaining boots-on-the-ground work at centers and case management agencies conducting intake and screening for housing supports through home visits.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about non-internet seniors and homebound outreach

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then you also said that you guys do outreach in the media.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How does DFTA ensure that older adults who make lack of internet or technology skills are not left behind in outreach and the application process?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Again, a lot of the work that happens on the ground at our centers, as an example, or with our case management agencies,

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: that's where we're reaching folks who are often some of the most vulnerable, who need the hands-on support with someone next to them to complete the application, to follow up and work with our colleagues at the Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: That's where the real boots on the ground, as you know, and work is happening.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: For the homebound seniors, what's a way you guys do outreach to those people?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Our case management agencies, as you know, again, over 30,000 individuals enrolled in the program.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: There's an intake.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: process for case management and folks to confirm that folks are homebound and they need support with various activities of daily living.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: One of the things that we screen for is whether or not they're eligible for a variety of housing supports.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So that work happens on the ground with our 21 case management agencies.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether DFTA partners with Meals on Wheels to deliver SCRIE information during meal deliveries, and Murray explains case management agencies handle home visits and applications, while home-delivered meals can also disseminate information.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about Meals on Wheels partnership for outreach

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you guys able to partner, say, meal on wheel when they're doing deliver the meal and give them the information and then help them to fill out the application there or they have to?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do some where else?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Yeah, typically the case management agency is responsible for helping with getting the application.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Home visits is a part of that, following up on applications where they have the authorization to complete those applications with the client.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And, of course, if one of the channels, if we need to make sure that we, through our home-delivered meals program, are disseminating information, that is also a channel.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: But our case management agencies are direct contact with the individuals who are homebound and are making sure that they're screening for and supporting applications.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether the Cabinet for Older New Yorkers works on SCRIE enrollment, and Murray describes two initiatives: PEU outreach and training Adult Protective Services staff to complete applications for the most vulnerable individuals.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about Cabinet for Older New Yorkers and SCRIE enrollment

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is green enrollment something the cabinet for older New Yorkers are working on?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: What I'll say is that, so Department of Finance and 311 and Department of Social Services are part of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: As you know, there are over 30 agencies.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: and we're continuing to expand.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: One of the initiatives, there are two initiatives that we did in the last few years.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: One was, as the first deputy commissioner shared, the outreach that happened directly through the mayor's...

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: of public engagement, another member of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And then the second initiative that we worked with are colleagues at APS, the Adult Protective Services, where some of the most vulnerable individuals, Department of Finance has trained APS to make sure that those applications are

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: as complete as possible and updated information.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So those are two initiatives that we've worked with our cabinet member agencies on.

chapters.summary: Zhuang questions the cabinet meeting schedule, noting a gap from a couple months ago to December, and Murray corrects that liaison meetings are monthly with the last executive cabinet meeting June 25th and the next on September 28th, and offers to follow up on publicizing agendas.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about cabinet meeting frequency and publicizing agenda

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When is the last time you got meat?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Our last cabinet meeting, I think, was the last couple months.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: And we meet quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When is the following meeting?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: I believe it's in December.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: December?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So you said a couple months ago, and then December, that's a half year.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it just happened, so I think the next meeting is in December.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: But we could follow up with the exact date for you.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: I'll get it before we leave today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: But it's a quarterly meeting.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Quarterly?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is that agenda can be publicized?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: I'll follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then let's turn the...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Shirley, you ready to ask questions?

chapters.summary: Jeffrey Shear adds that DOF's outreach unit, which conducts over 220 events annually, received over 1,200 SCRIE/DRIE applications in fiscal year 2026, up from 900 in fiscal year 2024, often completing applications directly with citizens at events.
chapters.title: DOF adds info on outreach unit application numbers

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: add that our outreach unit, which partners very

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: very frequently with the Department for the Aging, does assist

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: citizens in the field to complete their applications and oftentimes takes the applications directly from them so they do not have to submit them

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear

utterances.text: at which screen injury is at the top of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They often assist

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: so in fiscal year 26 that outreach staff received over 1200

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether agencies use dedicated ethnic media budgets for outreach, and Shear says applications are available in all required languages online but needs to follow up on foreign language media spending, while Hanif offers to recommend ethnic media outlets.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about ethnic media outreach budget and strategy

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then just in terms of keeping on topic with the outreach portion, I'm just going to skip around in my questions a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But I know that to Councilmember...

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: To Chair Zhuang's point, in terms of the media, one of the things that I believe used to happen, and I'm not sure if it's still happening, is that each agency has, I believe, a dedicated budget for local ethnic media.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so can you sort of talk about how that's been incorporated in a lot of the outreach efforts that you're working on?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear

utterances.text: I can say that our events are held in all five boroughs, all over the city, and that

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how DFTA reaches older adults outside the older adult center network, and Murray discusses community partnerships, subway campaigns on ageism and caregiving, and plans to proactively reach people entering their 60s.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DFTA outreach beyond OAC network

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: with current previous commissioners is that we know there are a certain number of folks that are coming to the OACs, but what about the seniors and older adults outside of that network, and how do we draw them in more?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about coordination with the Office of Mass Engagement and budget allocated for older adult outreach, with Murray confirming PEU is part of that office, and Shear offering to follow up on budget data.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about mass engagement and budget allocation

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then just, and this is for all of you, have there been conversations with the administration?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Because I know that there's the community of mass engagement, right?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so when I think of mass engagement, I think, how do we reach out to as many New Yorkers as possible to make sure that they are in the know of all the things that the city are doing?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so is that part of the conversation at all?

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: So in my testimony, I mentioned PEU, Public Engagement Unit.

utterances.speaker: Ryan Murray
utterances.text: That is part of the Office of Mass Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then how much of, do you know, in terms of the budget is allocated?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: For the older adult community.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I don't know if it's separated out that way, but if you could let us know, that'd be great.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't follow the question.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Just I wanted to see in terms of the amount of resources that are being dedicated towards certain issue areas or communities or demographics.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I was just wondering if there was any sort of data on that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about renewal rates and how many benefits lapsed for non-renewal between 2023 and 2025, and Shear reports a 95% renewal rate maintained through two letter reminders and four email reminders, with 70% of non-renewals due to late or missed deadlines.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about SCRIE/DRIE renewal rates and lapses

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then just in terms of the certification and renewal process, because I've been seeing, even just with the constituent casework coming into our district, some of the questions I'm going to be bringing up are

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: directly related to that, and others are more general.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But in terms of the certification renewal process,

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: How does DOF determine the screen dream multi-year benefit period?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I'm not sure screen injury is an annual benefit, and so I'm not sure I'm following the question.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So how do we ask this in a different way?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I'm trying to think of what the better way to ask this is.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So let me go into the rates, actually, and I'll come back to that one.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So what are the screen injury renewal rates and how many benefits lapsed for non-renewals between 2023 and 2025?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then how many were later restored?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So the renewal rate has been 95% over the past three years.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We're able to maintain this high rate with the help of two letter reminders and four email reminders to participants in the program.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Sorry, I just wanted to also note we've been joined by Councilmember Aviles.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about the most common reasons for missed deadlines, and Shear explains DOF doesn't hear from most non-renewing participants who may have moved, but sends reminders before and after deadlines with a grace period, and works with PEU on targeted outreach.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about reasons for non-renewal and follow-up

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, of the benefits that were not renewed, how many were due to late or missed renewal deadlines as compared to recipients no longer meeting program eligibility requirements?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, so 70% of the non-renewed benefits were due to late or missed renewal deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And that's 2237 out of 3,204 and 967 were not renewed due to participants no longer meeting eligibility requirements.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And for the ones that missed the date or due deadline, what is the sort of more popular reason, I guess you could say, like what's the most common reason why?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I believe that their incomes are too high.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Right, so those are for the ones that no longer meet the program eligibility requirements?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I understand, right.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But then for the ones that were late, was it because, I don't know, something, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Right, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In most instances, we, despite our efforts, we do not hear from these participants.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They may have moved.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are not in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, and so there's, I'm assuming there's no follow-up then?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So in other words, if you have a participant that just didn't renew.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So there is follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we are, we send two letters to them.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Both before and after the deadline, because there is a grace period where people who miss the deadline can still continue their benefits.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we send, for email, reminders both before and after the deadline, because we very much want to have people renew.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We're pleased that the renewal rate is 95%, and we are working to make it higher.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether DOF would support codifying automatic renewals to reduce lapses, and Shear explains current law doesn't authorize automatic renewals but DOF has created a short form for five-time renewers, and is willing to have conversations about automatic renewal if state law changes.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about codifying automatic renewals

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then do you have a stance on codifying automatic renewals for screen injury to reduce the lapses due to paperwork delays or processing of submissions?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I didn't get the...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: First part of that, do we have, have we?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Just codifying automatic renewals, yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So automatic renewals are not authorized by the current law.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: What there is, is for long-time participants, I think people who have had five renewals,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: their renewals can be done via a short form, and we have developed a short form for them to ease the renewal process.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, and would you be in favor of codifying it so that it is automatic?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That would require state legislation.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yes, no, I know.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But I just wanted to know how the department is, if it would be in favor of it if the law were to change.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I think we're willing to have a conversation about it.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We would like to consider that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many disability-related reasonable accommodation requests were received, granted, and denied, and Shear reports 190 SCRIE requests in FY25 with 3 denied and 202 in FY26 with 2 denied, plus 41 DRI requests in FY25 with 2 denied and 72 in FY26 with 0 denied.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about disability-related extension requests

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And how many disability-related extension requests were received, granted, and then denied?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Okay, so.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For SCRI, in fiscal year 25, we received 190 what we call reasonable accommodation requests.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And in fiscal year 26, we received 202 reasonable accommodation requests.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Of those, for fiscal year 25, three were denied.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So more than 99% were approved.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And for fiscal year 25, only two of those were denied.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And is it normal for you all to have only around that number?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: It seems like around 200.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Requests.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: It seems low.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many DRI benefit takeover applications were denied because a surviving member wasn't listed on prior applications, and Shear reports none, as DOF changed its policy in fiscal year 2022 to no longer deny for that reason.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DRI benefit takeover denials

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And how many DRI benefit takeover applications were denied because the surviving member had not been listed on prior applications?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And I do have information.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I gave you three statistics.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So just to fill out the information for 2025, we received 41 reasonable accommodation requests relating to DRI.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Two of those were denied.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And in fiscal year 2026, we received 72 reasonable accommodation requests and zero of those were denied.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, and I say this, maybe this is just because I'm not as familiar, but that number seems extreme.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: extremely low.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so do you know, is it because folks are not understanding that they can apply for some of these benefits or exemptions or?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Well, to be clear, these are people who come to us who say that they have not been able or will not be able to make the deadline due to a, typically due to a disability.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So it is only a small set of the applications that we are receiving.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Most people are able to come to us with timely applications.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then of the, and this is in the world where people have their applications in, and do you have any sort of data or statistics on how many people have, that still could apply for certain benefits but maybe have not, and what the outreach is like there?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do issue a report that estimates how many are eligible,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: but I want to emphasize that the mayor has been clear that he believes it is essential that we work hard to connect New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: to the services and programs available to them that can help make life in New York City more affordable.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That is why we continue to do extensive outreach for the rent freeze program in communities throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we do have a report, but the mayor wants us to be doing extensive outreach regardless of what's in that report.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we are committed to doing that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: No, and I have no doubt that you're committed to doing that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I'm just trying to think, as we're going through these questions, trying to think through some creative ways of how to expand the pie, I guess, so to speak, or expand the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then how many DRE benefit takeover applications were denied because the surviving member had, oh, I just asked that, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't get to answer that.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So please.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And the answer is none.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Do you?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: COF changed its policy on this in fiscal year 2022, so we are no longer denying any for that reason.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, perfect.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many benefits ended because household income temporarily exceeded $50,000 and how many had frozen rent restored, with Shear reporting SCRIE losses of 27 in FY24, 17 in FY25, and 8 in FY26, and DRI losses of 2, 1, and 1 respectively, promising to follow up on restoration data.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about temporary income exceedance data

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So state law allows a household that loses the benefit for excess income to reapply the next calendar year and have its prior frozen rent restored up to three times.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: For FY 2024 through 26, separately for scree and jury, how many benefits ended because the household income temporarily exceeded $50,000?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And also how many households had their prior frozen rent restored under that provision?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So the numbers I have are for, yes, for benefits that were ended because the household income temporarily exceeded $50,000 for

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: SCRI in fiscal year 2024-27.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2025, 17, and in fiscal year 2026, 8.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For DRI, the numbers are in fiscal year 2024, 2, in fiscal year 2025, 1, and in fiscal year 2026, 1.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I need to get back to you regarding the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hanif requests updated eligibility estimates for FY26-27 by borough, and Shear provides 2023-based estimates: 40,000 Manhattan, 37,000 Brooklyn, 30,000 Bronx, 27,000 Queens, and 1,400 Staten Island, noting methodology limitations that tend to overstate eligibility.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about eligibility estimates by borough

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then I know you sort of alluded to this in one of the previous answers, but if you could get back to us, because I think what would be curious for us to look at is we would want to know

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: what your estimates are for the eligibility for SCRI and DRI for FY26 and 27

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: in terms of like overall New Yorkers, how many would be eligible, and of those, how many actually are enrolled citywide and borough by borough, if you could give us that data if you don't have it now and as follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But if you have it, that'd be great.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So the last data we have relies on data for 2023.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay, so not 26 and 27?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We only do this estimate, and I want to emphasize that it is an estimate.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are relying on data regarding rent controlled or rent regulated units and income data that we're matching.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So it is not precise.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We also know that there are issues with the methodology, so we believe that it tends to overstate the number of eligible households.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: For example, accounting for households that might have more than one income tax filer in it is difficult for us to do.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And I do have numbers by borough.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: These numbers exclude numbers attributable to rent control and Mitchell Lama housing, but they are 40,000 for Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That's total.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So that includes households that are in the program and households that are not in the program.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: 37,000 for Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: 30,000 for the Bronx, 27,000 for Queens, and 1,400 for Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, if at all possible, if there's any way, because I, understanding that the methodology and everything is probably off a little bit, it'd be great to see if we can get updated numbers, only because I would say in that time period since 23,

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: especially the older adult community and certain populations have definitely grown quite a bit, and so I just want to make sure that we're capturing these numbers accurately, and then

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Before I hand it back, I just wanted to ask a couple questions about the enrollment.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether SCRIE and DRIE enrollment declines have different causes, and Shear attributes declines primarily to COVID-related deaths and people moving out of the city, noting a slight 0.8% enrollment increase in 2024.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about enrollment decline factors

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Because as I think was mentioned, screen enrollment fell from 63,000 in 2019 to 56,665 in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Is the decline in screen enrollment due to different factors compared to the decline in DRE enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And if they are different, what are the factors and what does this mean for outreach and enrollment efforts?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, we believe that, or we don't have,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: sufficient information to know all of the details behind the changes in enrollment that you and the other chairs have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do know that tragically during the pandemic, many senior citizens

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: fell seriously ill or passed away due to COVID, and that many New Yorkers did move out of the city.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we believe that these external factors have largely determined the decline in enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We're heartened by the fact that enrollment did increase, even though it was under 1%, but did increase this past year.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'm just wondering if there are other things factoring into that.

chapters.summary: Hanif raises concerns that public charge fears and immigration policy changes may be driving enrollment declines among immigrant seniors, and asks whether DOF tracks this, with Shear noting DOF doesn't ask immigration status but will look into the issue with community partners.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about immigration status impact on enrollment

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: For example, I know that when public charge happened back after 2016, a lot of older adults with legal immigration status even that we saw got off whatever benefits they were on because they were afraid of their immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And I know that HR1 and other things that are happening impact that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so I just wanted to know if there's a way to track that and also knowing that, how are we going to sort of shore up what we can and cannot do on the city level?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So I'd be interested to see, and again, if you could follow up and come back to us, if there's a way to see how those impacts are sort of factoring into the enrollment numbers here or if at all.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: That was just something we wanted to follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will look into that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do have challenges.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Obviously, we do not ask the immigration status of people who are applying to the programs.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Yes, that I know.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But especially with community partners on the ground, I think narratively speaking at least and somewhat like...

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Even with the OACs, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: or they'll be able to tell you what some of the challenges are.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so I'm just curious to see if there's any sort of data that is correlated with that and then in response on the city side what we can and should be looking to do.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So that was just the question there.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And I have a bunch more, but I'm going to pause here to allow our other co-chair as well as members to ask questions.

chapters.summary: Lee asks Commissioner Agarwal how MOPD participates in DRIE outreach, and Agarwal describes website information, constituent referrals through tabling and presentations, housing resource guidelines, and referrals to DOF's Disability Service Facilitator and PEU's Rent Freeze team, noting plans to enhance outreach including home access community engagement.
chapters.title: Lee asks MOPD about DRIE outreach and enrollment process

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I like to start with MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And give our Deputy Commissioner Shearer a bit of a break.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Commissioner Agarwal, could you share how MOPD participates in the outreach and enrollment process for DRE eligible New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: First of all, thank you to everyone to invite me here.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: Broad picture, this is an affordability issue, and New Yorkers with disabilities face the highest true cost of living against other populations in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: They also face the greatest

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: resource gap between actual income and true cost of living, nearly double the citywide average.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: So with that in context,

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: of the outreach we have done so far, and then I'll talk about what we want to do further.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: We have information on DRI in our website.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: As New Yorkers can reach out, see that in the website.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: We also, MOPD refers constituents seeking housing services, including DRI information.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And there's two ways we do that.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: One, MOPD proactively shares information about DRI programs through

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: tabling, presentations, or just talking to folks.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: So this morning I just got a constituent who met me in the Deaf Town Hall on Wednesday, and she wanted to talk about history.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: So that's like a way that we engage.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: We also have calling and emails, and we receive many emails about housing resources, and we share that to constituents as well.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: MOPD includes DRI in our housing resource guidelines, which is provided at outreach events to community partners.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: Like other people have said, if people need assistance and applications, we refer them to the Disability Service

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: Facilitator in Department of Finance and the Front Read.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: Brent Rees out in PAU.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: So those are all of the things we've currently been doing.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: Moving ahead, I think MOPD is seeking to enhance our DRE outreach and information dissemination efforts because this is the

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: mayor's affordability agenda, and so we want to expand that.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And the most, the biggest barrier we've noticed is that people with disabilities face

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: tend to not have access to information.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And we are committed to providing that information to the communities that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: For example, we are doing a home

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: access community engagement, disseminating information and answering questions about a range of housing resources, but that includes DREAM.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And we are also going to work with our city partners here, like

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: example, working with aging department.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And, you know, we are, we're very overlapped between the communities that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: And so working with aging, we can maybe move that ball forward.
