chapters.title: Brewer asks about memory loss and recertification challenges

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One more question quickly for Dree or Scree, which is we find a lot of people get older, they're forgetful, and they forgot to re-register, and they forget about Scree, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This is an increasing problem.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how are you going to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, say, for instance, we do the outreach, and we're getting more people to sign up and so on, but they do forget.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So is there something we can do that's more pre-populated?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It could be like I'm making more than one year.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm asking because increasingly you're going to get this memory loss, you're going to get people are not doing the right paperwork, etc.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then you have got the owner involved, you got the re-woman involved, you got the legal official involved, you got finance involved.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's a whole thing that goes on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I don't know how we can avoid.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm looking for suggestions from you and maybe from DIFTA.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, so we do some pre-population in our forms to help people.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And I mentioned earlier that we do quite a few reminders.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I'm sure we can look into that and come up with other thoughts as well.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I mean, that's where we're getting challenges.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So people are...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Forgot that they even needed to do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I assume that also happens in DRI for whatever medical challenge they're facing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I do think we need to look at it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You've got this huge number of more people getting older, and we need to think about this.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I also do want to reference back to the discussion about the reasonable accommodations that we supply specifically to...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: People in the programs, maybe older people with memory losses.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So that is set up precisely to assist those people.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I think more conversation along that line.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zhuang notes her office sees 7,000 people annually and urges DOF to offer workshops in all council member offices, and Shear confirms DOF wants to work with every member and sent outreach emails to all elected officials in August.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about expanding clinics to all council members

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also, I have a question from my district also.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: You guys have been working close with Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I think the other 50 council members also want you guys to have a workshop in their office too.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Please, we want to do it with you.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: You can contact me directly.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I do want to mention that we did an email campaign in August where our outreach staff sent emails to every New York City elected official,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: council members, state assembly members, and state senators, and also to some of their key staff, chief of staffs.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Heads of constituency work.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we want to be working with you.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We welcome the effort.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Call us.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, we definitely, my office sees 7,000 people a year.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: More than most of congressional district because people all over the city, if they speak Chinese, they think I'm their council member.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They will come to my office.

chapters.summary: Zhuang reads a question from Council Member Brooks-Powers about how many additional homeowners could benefit from raising the SCHE/DHE income ceiling to $75,000, and Shear estimates roughly 5,000 households citywide but doesn't have borough breakdowns.
chapters.title: Zhuang reads Brooks-Powers question on SCHE estimates

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah, so I have a question from Councilmember Brooks Power.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Her question is, my district in Southeast Queens has one of the highest concentrations of senior black homeowners in the city.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: For three and three, how many additional homeowners citywide and by borough does DOF estimate?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Estimate could benefit from raising the ceiling to 75,000.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Our estimate is roughly 5,000 households.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: In Southeast Queens?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Citywide.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Citywide.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I don't have a breakdown by borough or by neighborhood for that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What outreach efforts, especially for the other borough homeowners, could the DOF conduct to ensure that current and potential eligible SHRI recipients are aware of increased examination

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: percentage valuable under this bill?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, well, I do want to again point back to our existing significant outreach efforts that we've been discussing, the 220 events

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: annually, the work with MOPD, Department of Aging, but we also

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: in connection with this bill, Intro 978A, are having conversations with the Office of Management and Budget regarding what resources

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: would be needed to get the word out and to process the additional applications that we would expect.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether there are plans to address seniors in NYCHA or with Section 8 vouchers who are excluded from rent freeze programs, and Shear explains the state legislation only changes the income cap and doesn't alter basic eligibility guidelines.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about NYCHA and Section 8 exclusion from rent freeze

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And the second question, many of my lowest income seniors live in NYCHA or use a Section A voucher.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: are excluded from rent freeze program entirely.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: As the city expanding eligibility, is there any plan to address the senior who fell outside these programs altogether?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How else can we do more to meet their needs?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The state legislation does not change the basic application of the program.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So it's focused on the income cap.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It doesn't change the basic eligibility guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So nothing else can do.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are always ready to have constructive conversations with the council and come up with ideas.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, go back to my question.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether there is a single consolidated public-facing intake point like Access NYC that flags SCRIE/DRIE eligibility alongside other benefits, and Shear describes DOF's online eligibility tool and application portal, noting under 20% of applications are online and many seniors prefer paper.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about consolidated intake and Access NYC integration

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is there a single consolidated public-facing intake point, access NYC or something similar that flags screen and tree eligibility alongside other benefits a household may qualify?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have on our website an eligibility tool and a single place for people to apply online.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I should mention along the lines of the discussion earlier that many seniors prefer to apply via paper.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So right now, under 20% of the applications we get are online.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But we love online applications.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That helps speed the process.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And we have done work to make sure that people can apply entirely online.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So my question is, that's access NYC.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Because my office sees 7,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sometimes when it's super busy, I also see constituents myself.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I did Shree and Dree, all the application myself before for constituents.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: A lot of time people don't know they are qualified.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do we have a system when they are applying for the other benefits?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Also mention to them, hey, you are qualified for Shree and Dree.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you want to apply?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do we have anything compromised with the other program?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I will need to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Because that will make sure people know that program easier and also

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: remind them if they're qualified.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's probably one of the ways to do outreach.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Because when access NYC, when you go into the portal, they're going to tell you what benefit you can apply.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's actually very helpful for a lot of seniors and also caseworkers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If we can put that inside there together, then probably will be benefit to a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's my opinion.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks about the responsibility split between DOF and state DHCR and whether prior council legislation expanding income limits produced projected enrollment increases, with Shear noting no confusion with DHCR and attributing enrollment declines to pandemic factors rather than legislation.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about state vs city implementation and prior legislation impact

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How does the city implement screen and the tree compared to state oversight rule?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Where does responsibility split between DOF and New York State DHCR?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Are there any gap between and the conflict for applications?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I'm sorry, conflict?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah, create a confusion.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I mean, confusion for applications.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that being an issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So there's no gap.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It's easy.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's always challenging.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But I am not aware of confusion because of DOHCR.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What has been the status and the impact of prior council legislation expanding free and free income limits, including whether it's

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: produced the enrollment increase projected at the time?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So unfortunately,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: During the pandemic, enrollment did decline in the programs.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't think that was attributable to council legislation, but factors beyond our control.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what IT improvements could reduce lapses and whether funding was requested, and whether there's a cross-agency system that flags SCRIE/DRIE eligibility when seniors apply for other benefits, with Shear noting DOF maintains a dedicated rent freeze portal and Agarwal offering to follow up on cross-agency integration.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about IT improvements and cross-agency data sharing

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What administrative or IT department could most improve process on the limited time, reducing claps?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Has funding been requested for this current or upcoming budget?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Did you guys request any budget for that?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: In the IT budget?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have a system, so for rent freeze, we have a portal that's dedicated to it, and we maintain and we make upgrades to it as needed.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I don't know if there's a specific budget for it, but...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like cross-agency.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like say if this senior, they may be eligible for the other senior benefits.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: In the same time, they can send more information to different city agencies that, oh, maybe qualifies green and green.

utterances.speaker: Nisha Agarwal
utterances.text: I will get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shirley Aldebol asks whether there could be a joint application process for SNAP and housing benefits, noting providers frequently hear this request from constituents.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about joint applications with SNAP benefits

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then, Shirley, you have questions?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay, actually, I just wanted to piggyback off that line of questioning, because one thing that we've been hearing a lot from the providers and the nonprofits that actually provide the services is that oftentimes it'd be really helpful if there are joint applications.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And one of the most common things, which I'm sure you have all heard as well, is, is there a way to

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: jointly apply for food stamp SNAP benefits as well as the housing piece of it, right?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because that's something that seems to overlap a lot and we heard that from a lot of our housing providers as well as a lot of our food providers.

chapters.summary: Lee raises the idea of using AI and cross-agency data sharing to identify people falling through the cracks, comparing it to a common app for benefits, and Shear expresses DOF's interest in joining those conversations, acknowledging the time tax on beneficiaries and providers from multiple forms.
chapters.title: Lee discusses AI and cross-agency data sharing for applications

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have to say, I know there's some controversy out there about the use of AI, but this is one area where I feel like I wonder if, and I've spoken to other agencies about this, is

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: is there a way for us to, and I get there's HIPAA, all of those things, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: We want to protect privacy.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I've spoken to deputy mayors and commissioners about figuring out if there's a way to, first of all, identify people not in terms of their actual identity, but coding it somehow.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then also on top of that.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because at least in the mental health space, for example, when I was chair of mental health, we, you know, every time I ask questions about Be Heard, right, you know, or folks that have comorbid issues, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: If I am homeless and I go into a shelter one day and then next month I have an episode and I end up at H&H Hospital Systems, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then next month after that, I go into and get picked up by an outreach street team because of my issues around substance use, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So how are we ensuring that people are not falling through the cracks and that our systems are communicating with each other somehow?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Right, and I get that the cross-agency meetings with all the teams are important and helpful, like in person, but I also wonder from a

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: data perspective, is there a way that we can make things more efficient with the application process?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: As well as

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: some of the frustrations that our providers are saying.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because same thing, you know, when I was working in social services and the nonprofit sector, you know, you have to, the work that the caseworkers need to do is very cumbersome.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And even folks and friends of ours, myself personally, who are professionals, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: They may be doctors, lawyers, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: They call me because they're like, don't you guys do work with helping, you know, seniors and older adults apply for Medicare, Medicaid, all these benefits?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I'm like, yes, because these are professionals who are like, this is so complicated because it's literally so sort of like spread out in terms of the areas that they need to look into.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I just wanted to emphasize that point and put it out there that I do think that we need to start maybe having these conversations at a city level to see what can be done,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: understanding, of course, that we do want to keep information private and data private.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I just wonder if it would help us be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, DOHMH is interested in joining those conversations with you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I think other city agencies would also need to be involved, but we are open.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Understand your point, right?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: There is a time tax on...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Beneficiaries and on providers with having to deal with multiple forms or forms that are longer than they need to be.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And also, I mean, just like with college applications, there's the common app.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: right, where you apply for multiple things at the same time, which I know she's nodding her head because, like, I'm not saying it has to be done that same way, but, you know, is there something where, you know, there's basic information that we can collect all at the same time and share with different agencies?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I think that would speed up potentially the process.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So things like that, I just feel like, you know, we need to do better to help folks out.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that you guys are on the same page, but we've got to figure out how to continue those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Lee asks whether DOF publishes enrollment, denial, and utilization data publicly, and Shear confirms the data is available and will be shared directly with the Council.
chapters.title: Lee asks about public data reporting on SCRIE/DRIE

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And really quickly, I just wanted to ask, actually, speaking of data,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So this is sort of going into the section of data transparency in the budget.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Does DOF publish screedry enrollment denial utilization data publicly?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I think you did mention this, but just for the record, if you could reiterate.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And if not, would the agency support a local law requiring the reporting?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which specific data?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Oh, just about the screed re-enrollments, denials, and utilization data, if it's available publicly on the website or...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The data I referenced is available.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will also share it with you directly.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Lee asks about annual tax expenditures, and Shear reports $178 million in FY26, $214 million projected for FY27, and $243 million projected for FY28, representing 20% and 14% growth respectively, based on OMB's June 2026 plan.
chapters.title: Lee asks about tax expenditure figures for SCRIE/DRIE

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And what has been the annual tax expenditure associated with the screen injury programs in each of the last three fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: What I have is in fiscal year 26,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: $178 million.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: This is for Screedry together.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The projected amount for fiscal year 27 is $214 million.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And the projected amount for fiscal year 2028 is $243 million.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: These figures are from the OMB June 2026 plan.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Why the big jump?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Wait, so 14, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You said in FY27?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then 243 in FY28?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's a 20% growth to 27 and a 14% growth for 28.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Lee asks about the projected effect of the Rent Guidelines Board's 0% adjustment on SCRIE/DRIE enrollment, and Shear says DOF hasn't done that specific analysis but notes 0% is better for the public and doesn't change the need for outreach.
chapters.title: Lee asks about RGB 0% rent adjustment impact

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And what is the projected effect of the Rent Guidelines Board's adoption of a 0% adjustment for one and two year leases, which starts on October 1st through September 30th of next year?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I don't have that specifically.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do know that with 0%,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: that's better for the public and it means that people's budgets will be less challenged.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We haven't done an analysis to

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: figure out what the impact would be on enrollment in screen injury.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We still feel there's an essential need for us to do outreach regardless of the increase or lack thereof.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The mayor has emphasized that we need to do that, so we are committed to doing that.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Lee asks about the $44 million estimated cost of raising SCRIE/DRIE income limits over FY27-30, and Shear confirms the estimate hasn't changed since the state budget, with 82% ($36 million) attributable to SCRIE and 18% ($8 million) to DRIE.
chapters.title: Lee asks about $44 million cost breakdown for income limit increase

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just lastly, the February 2026 financial plan, it estimated the cost of raising the screedry income limit at $44 million over FY's 2027 through 2030.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And the June plan added a separate ski-hee-dee-hee line.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: What part of the $44 million is attributable to scree and what part to dree?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And has the estimate been revised since the state budget was enacted in May 2026?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because I know some of those numbers changed maybe.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The numbers have not changed.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So it hasn't changed since the state budget?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It hasn't changed since the state budget.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's still $44 million.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: About 82% of the total cost, $36 million, is attributable to SCRI, and the remaining 18%, $8 million, is attributable to DRI.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: And as you indicated, right, that's over a period of several years.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Several years, yep.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'm going to pause there for now.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Oh, actually, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to pause there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks whether DOF provides SCRIE/DRIE training to other agencies, what topics are covered, and who facilitates, and Shear confirms training is provided to DFTA, MOPD, ACS, and HRA staff on eligibility and application processes, conducted by outreach unit and taxpayer advocate staff on an as-needed basis.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DOF training to other city agencies

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Lee.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Does DOF currently provide training concerning scree or dree to personnel at other city agencies?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We provide training to staff from Department for the Aging, MOPD.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We also, because we do outreach with ACS and HRA, we have done training there as well.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And is this a training that happens annually or how, what's the basis of?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do the training as the other agencies need it, on an as needed basis.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then what topics are covered?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I think just in general, the eligibility for the program

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: and the application process, the sorts of things, the training that is done is done for staff at those agencies that will be doing outreach events for us.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So it's geared to the interactions that the agency would have with potential applicants.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then who from DOF facilitates those trainings?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That would be staff from our outreach unit and also from our taxpayer advocates office.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then going back to the enrollment data that was shared, so re-enrollment peaked at 12,215 in 2019, 11,000

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: roughly in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And talking about the decline or the fall of applications, you mentioned COVID as one reason, which I think is very fair.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what analysis capacity DOF has to examine enrollment decline causes, particularly in the Bronx, and Shear provides detailed breakdown showing deaths accounted for 56% of the 1,203 decline, non-renewals 225, moves 250, and 23 transfers to SCRIE, noting DOF loses contact with those who leave.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about Bronx DRIE enrollment decline analysis

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Is there, what kind of analysis capacity does DOF have to really look at what's causing an enrollment fall, particularly in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, so we do have some more information regarding the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I want to preface that by saying there are limits.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So when people leave the program, we lose touch with them.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: They don't tell us why they are leaving the program.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But we have these figures regarding, let's see.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: No, so this is regarding the decline of 1,200.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So I think the figures you are referring to is that re-enrollment peaked at 12,215 in 2019 and was 11,012 in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we break it out this way.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That death was the largest reason for that decline, accounting for 669 of the 1,203.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That's 56%.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Non-renewals, 225.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So again, we don't know precisely the reason why people did not renew.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We're aware of 250 where tenants move residences, and we have 23 that transferred to the SCRI program.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then for the...

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: The non-renewals,

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Is there reason not to check in?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Well, we do check in.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: What mostly happens is we do not hear anything further.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We're very intent on making sure that people in the program who remain eligible renew.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's very important for DOF that they renew.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are proud of the fact that we have 95% retention rate, and we do that by sending many reminders.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Paper letters, emails, and also working with PEU with lists of people who have not yet responded.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Understood.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how many DRI recipients are 62 or older, and Shear reports 6,729, offering to provide a breakdown of younger recipients as well.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DRI recipient age breakdown

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share how many DRI recipients are 62 or older?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: It's, I have that here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I believe it's roughly 6,200.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Oh, here we go.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then do you have a breakdown of folks who are younger?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: No, but we can come up with one.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I might be reaching my final questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So if you will give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I believe you may have answered this earlier.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how DOF reaches immigrant and limited English proficient communities, and Shear describes translated forms on the website, language translation services at five DOF business centers used about 120 times per month, and work with community-based organizations.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about immigrant and LEP community outreach

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: How are you reaching immigrant and limited English proficient communities?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Is this through community-based organizations?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do work with community-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We do provide translations of our forms on the website in many different languages.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We also have language translation services available at DOS five business centers, one per borough.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have stats showing that our exemption unit uses those services about 120 times per month.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Now, that's for all exemption programs.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: That's not specific to rent freeze, and I don't have the figure.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We don't provide breakdowns by program, but those are some of the ways in which we do that outreach.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And for the applications available in the other languages, are you all keeping track of, let's say, if I fill it out in the Bangla language?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Seven applicants have applied using that specific translated application, or how are you all tracking use?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So I need to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks where the five DOF business centers are located and whether applicants can walk in for application help, and Shear confirms one per borough with the Manhattan center on John Street having a dedicated exemption walk-in unit, while all centers provide translation services and application assistance.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about DOF business centers and in-person assistance

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then where are the five business centers?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: You said one in each borough?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: DOF has five business centers.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: I don't have the addresses on the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: One of them, the Manhattan Business Center, is walking distance from here on John Street.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We are one in Brooklyn is near Borough Hall.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We can provide you with the addresses for all five.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And at these business centers, are they so that applicants can drop in to get the support they need to fill out an application?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yeah, so...

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Yes, we provide additional support in our Manhattan Business Center.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So our exemption unit has a separate exemption walk-in unit.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So people can either walk in without an appointment or make an appointment in advance.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: So we have additional service there.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But for all of our business centers,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: People walk in, the business centers do a wide variety of service to New York City citizens, ranging from

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: parking ticket hearings, assisting people paying their property taxes, and everything and anything in between.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: People at the business centers.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We'll get people walking in who need assistance and we can provide them with translation services.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then when someone's applying specifically for SCRI or DRI, is that also where they can come in to do that, or are there other centers?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: The best place for people who want to have specific help with their application would be our Manhattan Business Center.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: But again, I want to emphasize that we provide the same type of assistance at many of our outreach events.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have outreach staff who know the applications and as indicated earlier, we

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: received, that staff received 1,200 applications in fiscal year 26,

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: precisely because we know that this population often needs hand-holding and can't do it online or can't do it on paper by themselves.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We have outreach that addresses that issue.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about the best way for the public to find out about DOF outreach events, and Shear says DOF contacts council members directly about events.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about how to find outreach events

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And then the best way to find out about these outreach events is how?

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: We will contact you directly, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I believe everyone sitting here, we have the same goal, help our seniors and the people with disability.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And as city council member, I believe everyone

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: All my colleagues sitting here want to provide resources to the agency also.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Let's serve our seniors and disabled community together.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's our goal.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It's not someone did something wrong.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This is our goal, try to accomplish everything together.

chapters.summary: Zhuang thanks agency representatives, emphasizes shared goals of serving seniors and disabled communities, and announces the transition to public testimony.
chapters.title: Zhuang closes Q&A and transitions to public testimony

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, I want to thank everyone come here.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And now we're going to move to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jeffrey Shear
utterances.text: Thank you all.

chapters.summary: Zhuang reads public testimony rules including two-minute limits, no recording at the witness table, and written testimony submission procedures, then calls the first panel: Lloyd Feng, Molly Krakowski, Irak Shehansky-Rivas, and Ariel Hirsch.
chapters.title: Public testimony instructions and first panel called

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, I now open to the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I want to remind members of public that this is government proceeding and the decor shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: As such, members of public shall remain silent at all time.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: No video recording photography is allowed for the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recording as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sergeant at Arm for including in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with Sergeant at Arm and a way to recognize.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on the oversight topic, senior citizen rent increase exemption screen and the disability rent increase exemption tree, or

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: on any of the legislation on today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you have written testimony or additional written testimony you may wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arm.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Now we're going to call our first panel.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The first one is Lloyd Fang.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Molly Korkoski.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Wing, purse, saw me.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Iraq, Sianki, Rivers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Ariel Harris.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Harris.

chapters.summary: Lloyd Feng of AARP New York, representing 750,000 city members, supports raising the SCRIE/DRIE income threshold from $50,000 to $75,000, citing a 2025 report showing 41% increase in older adults in poverty and 250,000 older New Yorkers below the poverty line.
chapters.title: Lloyd Feng testifies for AARP supporting Intro 978

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Thank you, Committee Chair Zhuang and Co-Chair Li and members of the Committee on Aging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: My name is Lloyd Feng, and I am the Associate State Director of Advocacy for AARP New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: I'm here today on behalf of our 750,000 members in New York City and the millions of older adults who called the city home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: We're here to support Intro 978, which would raise the maximum threshold income eligibility for SCRI and DRI from $50,000 to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: As you know, older New Yorkers are working harder today to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Our 2025 report with the Center for an Urban Future reveals the dire financial crisis facing older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Over the past decade, the number of older adults living in poverty increased by nearly 41%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Today, more than 250,000 older New Yorkers live below the poverty line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: That same report finds that nearly 60% of New Yorkers over age 70 reported no retirement income at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the number of New Yorkers age 65 and older who are working increased.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: So after a lifetime of contributing to the city, older New Yorkers deserve better than to be left behind by it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: If we want New York City to remain a place where people can afford to grow older, our policies must wake up to the harsh realities older adults face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Raising the eligibility threshold is a logical, necessary, and compassionate step to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: AARP New York has long advocated for strengthening and expanding SCRI and DRI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Increasing eligibility is critical to ensuring these lifelines keep pace with the cost of living and serve more of the people they were created to protect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: We urge the Council to pass Intro 978 now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lloyd Feng
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

chapters.summary: Molly Krakowski of JASA, serving 40,000 older adults, supports expanding SCRIE/DRIE eligibility and urges robust multilingual outreach, requiring housing providers to post eligibility information, and proactively reaching out to those previously denied for exceeding $50,000 income.
chapters.title: Molly Krakowski testifies for JASA on implementation priorities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: Chairs Schwing, Lee, and Hanif, and your respective committees, thank you so much for hosting today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: My name is Molly Krakowski.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: I'm Senior Director of Government Affairs at JASA, and very happy to be here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: JASA is one of New York City's largest and most trusted agencies serving older adults for nearly 60 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: We provide comprehensive network of services to more than 40,000 older adults across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: Housing stability is essential to that mission and to our mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: And older adults we serve are facing rising rents, property taxes, food costs, utilities, and other expenses, often on very limited incomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: Being able to remain in their homes, in the community, can make the big difference between continuing safely and independently or facing displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: Jess is very pleased to see the expansion of the income eligibility for SCRI and DREA, and we support many of the proposals before the committee today and submitted written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: But we wanted to highlight just a few of the priorities for implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: First, expanded eligibility will only help if people know about it, and I think we heard plenty today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: The city needs to make a robust multilingual outreach central to implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: It's not enough to just use the older adult centers and community-based organizations, but housing providers, social service agencies, other trusted sources, landlords, property managers should also be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: required to post information about the new eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: We're especially encouraged the Department of Finance is going to, we would especially encourage the Department of Finance to proactively reach out to people who were previously denied because their income exceeded the $50,000 threshold.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: There are people in the city that they know about who may already be qualifying and they should not have to navigate the process to find out on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: We also want to emphasize that even an older adult who's earning $75,000 may still face significant financial pressure in New York City, so we encourage the city

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: to continue looking at the needs of older adults and people with disabilities who remain just above those eligibility thresholds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: And I will submit written testimony so you can hear more, but we've heard a lot today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Molly Krakowski
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Irak Shehansky-Rivas of the New York State Association for Affordable Housing supports Intros 307, 934, 978A, 1010, and 1033, and Resolutions 55, 470, 512, and 431, urging adequate agency staffing and resources to prevent eligible New Yorkers from waiting for relief.
chapters.title: Irak Shehansky-Rivas testifies for NYSAFA supporting bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon, Chair Schwang, Chair Lee, Chair Hanif, and members of the Committee on Finance, Aging, and Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: My name is Irak Shehansky-Rivas, New York City Policy Director at the New York State Association for Affordable Housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify on behalf of our membership today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: For 28 years, NYSAFA has represented the for-profit and not-for-profit developers, owners, and managers who build, finance, and operate affordable housing across New York State.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: Many of our members serve senior citizens and people with disabilities who rely on screen and read to remain stably housed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: NISAFA supports introductions 307, 934, 978A, 1010, and 1033 together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: These bills streamline application and recertification, raise income eligibility thresholds, and make notice requirements more workable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: We also support resolutions 55, 470, 512, and 431, calling on Albany to establish automatic enrollment, expand re-eligibility beyond the head of household, protect benefits after a temporary increase on income,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: and incentivize preservation of housing for seniors and people experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: As these measures move forward, we encourage clear eligibility standards, efficient administration, protections for taxpayer information, and timely notice to property owners when exemptions change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: Because this hearing is oversight of the city implementation of recent SCRI reforms, we also urge that reforms be paired with adequate agency staffing and resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: So, eligible

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: New Yorkers aren't left waiting for relief they already qualify for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: We will submit our full written testimony, which addresses each bill and solutions in more detail for the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Irak Shehansky-Rivas
utterances.text: Thank you for your leadership on these issues.

chapters.summary: Ariel Hirsch of UHAB urges passage of the full suite of bills, focusing on Intro 978A and Intro 307's impacts on HDFC and Mitchell-Lama cooperatives, citing cases of seniors waiting months for SCRIE approval through HPD's paper-only process and language barriers in documentation requirements.
chapters.title: Ariel Hirsch testifies for UHAB on HDFC and Mitchell-Lama impacts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Good afternoons, Chair Zhuang, Hanif, Lee, thank you for holding today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: My name is Ariel Hirsch, and I am the Director of Policy at UHAB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: For over 50 years, UHAB has helped low- and moderate-income New Yorkers become homeowners in the buildings where they already live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We provide technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: assistance and training to 1,200 HDFC cooperatives and 24 HCR supervised Mitchell-Lama co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: And we're here today to urge the council to pass basically the full suite of bills, but I want to focus my testimony specifically on 978A and Intro

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: 307 and talk a little bit about how they impact HDFC shareholders and Mitchell-Lama shareholders specifically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: I think Intro 978, we've talked a lot about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We need to update this to be in line with state law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: It is a cruel thing to be on a fixed income but not poor enough to be protected from rising carrying charges, especially in a place with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: rising inflation and compounding operating and carrying charges that put cooperatives, Mitchell-Lamas, HDFCs, in particular vulnerabilities for their overall financial and physical health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Intro 307 would make it easier for residents to apply and keep their benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: HDFC and Mitchell-Lama cooperators, as we heard earlier, are still using paper applications with HPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: I think we talked a bit about Mitchell-Lama.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We talked a little bit less about HDFC co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We work with many, many folks working through SCRI and RE applications and recertifications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: A few just sort of standout examples.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We've been working with a senior who's been trying to apply for SCRI since February of this year and still has not received approval.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: We understand there is one person in HPD asset management approving these HDFC applications and is wildly...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: oversubscribed for the amount of requests they are getting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: And we're also working with a senior who needed to provide additional IRS documentation for their SCRI application and had real difficulties procuring this due to language barriers, lack of support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Overall, we can do a lot, but we can only do so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: And we really need a focus in this overall legislative package on the ways that this impacts especially Mitchell Lama and HDFC cooperatives and the overall financial and fiscal health of their buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

utterances.text: Janine Cahill Jackson.
