chapters.summary: Katrina Toma of Legal Services NYC reports assisting nearly 1,200 families with SCRIE/DRIE from 2023-2025 and over 300 in 2026, noting many clients are ineligible due to the $50,000 cap and that household income rules pressure families to split up to qualify.
chapters.title: Katrina Toma testifies for Legal Services NYC on income threshold

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairperson Lee Zhuang and Hanif and members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: My name is Katrina Toma, and I'm an advocate representing individuals with disabilities at Legal Services of NYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to testify concerning Intro 978-A, which, if enacted, will increase the maximum income levels for screen injury

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: rent-freeze programs from $50,000 to $75,000 as permitted by the 2026-2027 state budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: Legal Services of NYC is the largest civil legal services provider in the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: We handle over 32,000 cases annually, benefiting 108,000 New Yorkers, including around 10,000 clients receiving Social Security, Supplemental Security Income, Social Security Disability Insurance, and 14,000 clients who are SANS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: From 2023 through 2025, LISNI assisted nearly 1,200 families, totaling more than 1,700 people, with obtaining screen injury benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: So far in 2026, we have assisted more than 300 households with these applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: However, many more...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: of our clients and other low-income people throughout New York are ineligible for screen injury benefits because their household income exceeds the current cutoff of $50,000 per year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: As a result, they are subject to rent increases at each lease renewal of their rent-regulated apartments despite often being on the fixed incomes, and many are subsequently priced out of their rent-regulated apartments despite the existence of the rent-freeze programs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: which were created precisely to avoid such an outcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: Since the screen injury income limits were last increased at $50,000 in 2014, the national inflation rate and the average cost of rent in New York City have skyrocketed, forcing low-income elderly and disabled

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: individuals to stretch their incomes further and further just to survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: Moreover, because eligibility is determined by household income, low-income families are often under significant pressure to split up their households to become eligible for a screen injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: Not only does this defeat the purpose of screen injury, it also threatens to take away critical support systems to elderly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katrina Toma
utterances.text: Fox.

chapters.summary: Elizabeth Fox of Brooklyn Legal Services shares a client case where a household earning $52,000 annually—$2,000 over the limit—couldn't freeze their rent despite being on fixed incomes and facing retirement, arguing expanded eligibility would prevent eviction and displacement.
chapters.title: Elizabeth Fox testifies on eviction cases and income limit gap

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairpersons and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: My name is Elizabeth Fox.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: I am a staff attorney in the right to counsel unit of the Brooklyn Legal Services, part of LSNYC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: In my role, I serve people on the brink of eviction and homelessness every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Our hardest cases in right to counsel are often cases pertaining to the exact populations that screen injury aim to serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Seniors and people with disabilities on limited incomes whose benefits or employment cannot keep up with inflation and the rising cost of rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Screen injury can be a lifeline for these New Yorkers, and expanding the income limit would allow more people to maintain affordable housing, especially those who may currently be able to afford their rent, but stand no chance of continuing to do so as their incomes plateau while their rents rise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Just this past spring, I assisted a client who I'll call Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: A, who would have greatly benefited from an increased maximum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: A had lived in her rent-stabilized apartment for around 14 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Despite being in her late 60s and dreaming of retirement, she was still working full-time to afford her rent and other expenses, earning around $39,000 per year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Her spouse, who was nearly 80 years old, homebound and requiring around-the-clock medical assistance, had a sole income from Social Security of around $13,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Their combined income put them at roughly $52,000 annually, which is about $2,000 over the limit for SCRI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: This meant that they were unable to freeze their rent at the time I was assisting them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Neither Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: A nor her spouse will ever make more money than they do now, and when Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: A retires and takes Social Security, her household income will be reduced to about half of what it currently is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Yet, without assistance, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: A will be unable to safely retire for fear of facing eviction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: This household deserves to be able to stay in their apartment, and expanding the income limits will allow them to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: The state of New York recognized that the current income limits create a cruel and unnecessary barrier to assistance when it permitted those limits to be raised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: These are essential programs that help some of the most marginalized communities in New York City maintain their housing stability, and raising the income maximum would greatly expand access to these benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Expanded eligibility would better reflect the economic realities facing today's seniors and people with disabilities and ensure that modest increases in income or benefits do not prevent individuals from accessing critical rent protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Stable housing is often the foundation for good health, financial security, and community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: When seniors and people with disabilities remain in their homes, they are better positioned to maintain medical care, remain connected to their support networks, and live independently with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Based on our experience serving low-income New Yorkers every day, expanding eligibility would help more individuals and their families maintain housing stability and economic security while meeting their other essential needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Fox
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Solomon Smart of Bronx Works supports Intro 978A and Resolution 55, citing data showing SCRIE/DRIE recipients save $176-$191 monthly over 5-10 years, and noting Bronx Works has served older adults since 1972.
chapters.title: Solomon Smart testifies for Bronx Works supporting bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: My name is Solomon Smart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: I serve as the Associate Vice President over Older Adult Services at Bronx Works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: And I'm happy to be here on behalf of Bronx Works in support of all the suite of bills here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: I particularly love to talk just in support of Introduction 978A and Resolution 55.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: We're all on the same team here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: I think I can't say anything really new.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: I was surprised by Councilmember Hanif's information regarding the Bronx numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: So I'm glad that we're doing this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: I found an interesting report from 2022 on the rent freeze that showed that people on scree and dree for five to ten years save about $176 to $191 a month, which

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: can amount to about $2,000 a year or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: And I don't think I need to emphasize how much that little bit of money would mean to older adults and disabled members of our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: And so we very much support this at Bronx Works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: We've been serving older adults since 1972.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: It's very dear to our hearts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Solomon Smart
utterances.text: So I thank the council for this meeting and for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Janine Cahill-Jackson of the Legal Aid Society shares a case of an 82-year-old Bronx tenant $3,000 over the income limit and facing eviction after heart surgery, who cried upon learning about the proposed income threshold increase, and urges passage of the bills.
chapters.title: Janine Cahill-Jackson testifies on 82-year-old client facing eviction

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: My name is Janine Cahill-Jackson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Elder Law for the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, for convening this hearing on these important issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: The Legal Aid Society supports all of the changes proposed to the program that will make it work better for our clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: But my testimony today will focus on the income increase for screen dry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: Just yesterday, I was in Bronx Housing Court representing an 82-year-old woman who is a rent-stabilized tenant for decades and just survived major heart surgery, but is facing eviction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: She grabbed my arm and looked in my eyes and started to cry because she knew her renewal lease was coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: She said, am I going to get the rent freeze?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: And I immediately asked her, why aren't you on screen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: And she shared her income information, and she was only $3,000 over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: And she says, but I can't get a job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: I'm only getting older.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: I have no one else to help me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: What am I ever going to do, even after this lease?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: I shared a little bit of the information about today's hearing, and she had a huge smile come across her face and said, well, I hope when my next lease expires, the council will pass the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: She's been struggling to decide between paying her full rent, cutting back on food, and paying for her necessary heart medications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: Had Scree kept up with inflation, she could have qualified years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: Other senior clients that we have are still working to save for retirement, so their income is a little bit too high, yet their rent continues to grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: So while they save, their most essential expense, rent, only continues to grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: With the lower rent burden, clients like these will be able to afford the other things that they need, not only a roof over their head.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: We support the bills and resolutions before the Council today, increasing access to scree and dree, including

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: the increase in income limits from $50K to $75K, helping low-income seniors and individuals living with disabilities like the clients I just described so greatly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: We will also be submitting written testimony on the rest of the bills and resolutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janine Cahill-Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Hopefully we can help your client.

chapters.summary: Jean Stevens of VOLS strongly supports Intros 307, 978A, and Resolutions 55 and 512, describing their rent freeze clinics and hotline, and arguing automatic enrollment, universal applications, and benefit restoration after temporary income increases would have immediate impact on the 57% of eligible New Yorkers who remain unenrolled.
chapters.title: Jean Stevens testifies for Volunteers of Legal Service

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: My name is Jean Stevens, and I'm the Director of the Benefits Law Project at Volunteers of Legal Service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much for this opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Vols strongly supports Introductions 307, 978A, 476, 2026, 55, 512, because we know firsthand that the population we serve desperately needs all of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: So the Benefits Law Project, we assist New Yorkers who rely on public assistance, including screen and tree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: All of our clients live below 200% of the federal poverty level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: We're one of the few legal services providers that focus specifically on screen and tree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Our goal is to reach the 57% of New Yorkers who are eligible for screen and tree but remain unenrolled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: We help them apply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: We help them to maintain their benefits so they can stay in their homes and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: And avoid eviction and displacement, as my colleague stated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: We host rent-free clinics all over the city where volunteer attorneys meet with clients to advise them on eligibility, help them apply and renew, also to troubleshoot any issues that come up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Our volunteers also assist clients who contact us through our hotline, and we at Foles also advocate to DOF and HPD on our clients'behalf to resolve any issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: So from our experience, we know why so many New Yorkers remain unenrolled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Anyone who assists with these benefits can see that it's very

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: challenging for anyone, even attorneys, to navigate the applications, all the required documents, even for many people we assist to find the application, which we've been talking about, let alone older adults and people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: The groups that this program is designed to benefit face the most challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: They cannot quickly research the correct application to submit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: They don't know how to find the documents they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: They don't know how to access a portal or email or follow up on deadlines or how they're going to absorb a financial increase in their rent when their income goes up just for one year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: So all of these bills we support because they address these issues head on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: They have an immediate impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: The increasing number of New Yorkers with incomes above $50,000 who live on that razor-thin line of affordability and precarity, paying more than a third of their income on rent, now they will be able to be eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Many more people will be eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: An automatic enrollment system would create an opt-out mechanism rather than an opt-in and provide overnight relief for thousands of eligible tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: It would save thousands of hours of stress for tenants and administrative headache for the city and cost for the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Similarly, a universal application and recertification would mean applicants won't be applying to the wrong agency and missing out on months of benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Those with children with disabilities could now benefit from DRI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: And then finally, those who do lose their screedry because of a temporary boost in income will then be able to get it back restored at their same frozen level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: For these reasons, we strongly urge the council to pass these legislative efforts to expand screen injury eligibility and streamline these processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I want to thank everyone to help our seniors, people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jean Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, we have next round is...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Susan Duquet.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Simon Geisker.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Walter Adler.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Walter Adler.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Omar Muhammad.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Michael O'Connor.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Michael O'Connor.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Christina, Christian, Christian Bar-Lopez.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Christian Bar-Lopez.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Nicholas Mosley.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Nicholas Mosley.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Alex Cardoza.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Cardone?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Cardone?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, when you guys ready, please speaking.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Suzanne Duque of FDNY EMS Be Heard office describes EMS workers' role in supporting vulnerable New Yorkers, their exposure to hazards, and the challenges of choosing between overtime and family needs on low wages.
chapters.title: Suzanne Duque testifies on FDNY EMS community work

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Suzanne Duque.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: I work for the FDNY EMS Be Heard office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: My views today do not necessarily reflect what the views of FDNY are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing me to testify today about the outreach work New York City EMS

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: are doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: Day by day, night by night, New York City EMS practice our part in supporting the caring, vibrant, resilient, inclusive city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: We help safeguard the universal right for health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: New York City EMS, their work is not necessarily seen as a social expenditure, but much more as an effort to reach the residents with the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: humanitarian goal of medicine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: New York City EMS step into dirt through roaches, through heat, through cold, through snow to reach the patients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: They are exposed to blood-borne pathogens and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: They connect and ease the hopelessness sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: They use their excellent skills in medical care and their people skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: And the community...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: The community participation is celebrating diversity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: But yet, we very often have to make the choice between going home and doing overtime, between help our own children go through school and making the money to pay for rent.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you didn't finish, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Suzanne Duque
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you for your work.

chapters.summary: David Cook of EMS PAC, an FDNY paramedic and lieutenant, describes critical ambulance shortages with 10-30 minute response times, low pay driving mass exodus from the field, EMS workers considering striking, and calls on the City Council to address the emergency staffing crisis, noting $50 million in state EMS funding was redirected to firefighters.
chapters.title: David Cook testifies for EMS PAC on staffing and pay crisis

utterances.text: Sorry to do this, I'm sorry.

utterances.text: First of all, I just want to say good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I'm a paramedic and I'm also an active lieutenant with the Fire Department of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Before we start, I want to say thank you to everybody in this room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The reason I'm saying thank you to everybody in this room is because I know what it's like to pick up patients who have disabilities and I want to tell everybody with disabilities, you are superheroes and you are inspiration to me and others and I want to say thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I know it's hard for you with disabilities, but I tell you, I respect you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I also...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Yeah, the EMS.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: EMS?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: No, no, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I also want to thank you guys as well because you guys, by making sure these elderly people get the money that they need, I know what it's like for these elderly patients who have Alzheimer's and other diseases, and they don't even have people to help them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: So the fact that you guys are going to be able to give them more income is phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I want to say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The reason why we're all here is these are a bunch of FDNY EMTs and paramedics and a bunch of Hospital 911 EMTs and paramedics, and they're super here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I want to say thank you to everybody on this panel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I represent EMS PAC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: We're a nonprofit organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: You can follow us on Instagram or Facebook.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The reason why we're here and we're here in numbers is because New York City has a crisis and it's an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And I'm being very honest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I didn't come here just to talk lollygag stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I'm being honest with you guys from the heart now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The truth is we do not have enough ambulances out there on the streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I've been with, let me give you my background first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I became an EMT in 2006.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I worked in New Jersey for Nationwide Ambulance and also Bell and Mobile Vital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I became an FDNY EMT in 2008.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I became a paramedic in 2010.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I got upgraded with FDNY as a paramedic in 2011.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I also won numerous EMS competitions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I was a paramedic instructor for New York Methodist Hospital, and I'm currently a paramedic instructor for LaGuardia College right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: So anybody who wants to be an EMT and paramedic, I suggest you come to LaGuardia, and I want to say thank you to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: At LaGuardia because they're phenomenal instructors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The reason why we're here is because I know what it's like to have to be in Brooklyn, and they'll call me for a cardiac arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: That means somebody's heart is not beating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to break things down simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: You have a bunch of cells in your body, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And guess what?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: In four to six minutes, when your heart stops, those cells start to die.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And guess what?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: When somebody's in Brooklyn and there's a cardiac arrest in Staten Island or there's a cardiac arrest in the Bronx and there's not enough ambulances, we need you guys on the council to help fix this because we also advocate for the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Now, the big thing that while we're here, too, is because we have issues beyond just not the retention rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The fact that we don't even have budget to get equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Kathy Hochul passed a bill for $50 million to get passed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I'm going to keep going out of your respect and my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Kathy Hochul passed a bill for $50 million for EMS, and the firefighters took that bill, and they took the money and used it for their equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: We do not have the right resources or the right enough manpower to get to you guys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And because of these issues with the low pay on top of that, I'm telling you guys right now, this is the emergency why we're here for New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: EMS is having talks now, and this is in all garages, every station to station, all the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: We do not care about the Taylor Law Act, and EMS people are talking, and they are considering to strike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And this is for Mandami and for City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And I'm telling you guys right now, you do not have enough resources as it is right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: People in New York City are dying every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: So I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I want you to put yourself in the situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: We're going to speak and be honest now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I want everybody to wake up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I don't care about egos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: The truth is, you go down right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: You want to hit the clock?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Call 911 and say somebody's heart stopped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I bet you it's going to be 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: FDNY's been lying up here with their stats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: It's not five to six minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: There's not enough ambulances and people are dying in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Guess who has to take the loss?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: It's us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: We take it home because we care about saving you guys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: So I'm telling city council, we had to crash the party because there's an emergency going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Yes, NEMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And this is for Mandami and all of you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: No disrespect, but it's for all of you and your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: I'm speaking to the people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: You took an oath.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: If somebody takes a flight from Florida to come see New York City for the first time and they drop dead, 20 minutes for an ambulance, 30 minutes for an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Imagine getting a cardiac arrest right here going to the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: How long do you think it's going to take for me to get there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: People are dying in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And I want to address FDNY personally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: FDNY is run by Commissioner Lillian Bonsignor, who under her administration was hired by Mandami.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: Guess what?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: She hasn't done anything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: She was the reason why COVID, hold on one second, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: She was the reason why COVID situations happen and other things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Cook
utterances.text: And I just want to say, no, no, thank you, thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Please respect other people's time.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I understand your concern.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also, we will address your issue later.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And this is for this hearing for senior.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I personally really appreciate all the EMS workers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And as a council member and with my colleagues, we also...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: understand EMS doesn't pay enough.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: EMS worker did not pay enough.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Your salary is very low.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: For me, it's a big issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But today we have hearing on screen and the tree.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We will have a separate, probably have separate hearing or something to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Councilmember, with all due respect, the reason why all of us are here is that the understaffing of EMS is leaving older and disabled New Yorkers highly vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: As David was mentioning, there are not enough ambulances in the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I've been an EMT for three years, and the response times are only increasing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It is incredibly difficult for us when we have to respond to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: a potentially life-threatening emergency, and we're half an hour away, and we know that person might not make it by the time we get there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: They might be in a really unstable or potentially unsalvageable condition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: All of us, you know, we don't want to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: How do I say this mildly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: There are simply not enough ambulances, EMTs, paramedics in the system to properly take care of people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And that is leaving New Yorkers vulnerable to a wide variety of conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We believe that there needs to be way more increase in training, increase of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: staffing for all EMS personnel, because the reason is right now for understaffed or normal operation level, think about when there's a crisis, when there's a natural disaster like a flood,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: a pandemic, a terrorist attack, then New Yorkers are going to be even more vulnerable to death.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just interject also, because I don't know if you all were at the finance hearing, the executive committee hearing in May,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: but there was, I would say, probably the longest portion of the testimony was focused on a lot of our EMS workers and how important pay parity is and salaries are.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I have to say the...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: The folks that were head of the agencies actually gave a very, in case you guys were all planning on saying this, because we do want to try to stick to screedry, but

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: they actually gave us very insightful information on exactly what you were saying about calls, ambulances having to be shifted around, and if one moves here, then there's a lack of one here, and then if there's a call here, and what that does in terms of response time.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And as former chair of mental health disabilities and addictions, be heard was something that was very important to me as a social worker.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I totally understand.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I actually went to the site in Bay Terrace that does the trainings in Fort Totten, and I have to say that was very eye-opening as well.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I understand the outreach teams are super, super critical.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so that is something that I just wanted to emphasize that on the council we've really been trying to fight for is increasing the salary levels of our EMT and EMS workers because we know how valuable you are.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I just wanted to say that up front because I know that, you know, for the public test.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: testimony portion, we do want to try to stick it to the topic.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But maybe if the chairs are okay, if we can maybe briefly have you just go through what you had written and then just respect the two minute time if possible.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Please only two minutes every time, every person, and also please stick on the topic.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I understand your frustration.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But today we are more focused on screen energy.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Walter Adler, a 23-year paramedic, expresses EMS support for all legislation benefiting elderly and disabled New Yorkers, explains EMS workers came to the hearing because only one or two committee meetings per year address EMS issues, and frames EMS as allies in fighting for affordable housing and vulnerable populations.
chapters.title: Walter Adler testifies on EMS solidarity with vulnerable New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: My name is Walter Adler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I'm a paramedic for a hospital-based 911 system in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I've been working in EMS for 23 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Let me raise and resolve on behalf of my colleagues who are here from the private sector, the hospital sector, and the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: That any legislation whatsoever that is beneficial to the elderly and disabled of our city, that helps them live lives with dignity and helps them survive, all 15,000 EMS, EMTs, and paramedics support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And I know that because I know the soul of the ambulance worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Which is to say I know that the men and women that sign up to become EMTs and paramedics are the kind of women that will go in every circumstance for when our aging members of our city are at their very worst moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: The legislation that you're proposing, we support, and we in no means seek to disrespect you or the council by bringing our issues before you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: 30 committee meetings that happen a month, maybe only one or two

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: are about EMS per year, and that is why for 30 years, nothing has advanced in our field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: EMS PAC, the Emergency Services Public Advocacy Council, is always going to stand by low-income New Yorkers, immigrant New Yorkers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: New Yorkers that want an affordable life in our city, and in that regard, our organization will always be on the side of the mayor and members of the council that are fighting for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: How I seek to make this relevant for today's topic, which is purely about aging, disabled New Yorkers getting more secure housing and a better life and opportunity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: is I want people to understand that EMS members are not just here to beg with our hands out for five more dollars salary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We see ourselves as agents of this city and as members that support the city's most vulnerable members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: So we're here today in solidarity, not just with our own wages and our own labor struggles, but to say we wish to be allies to ARP, to members of the council, to everybody fighting for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariel Hirsch
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Next one.

chapters.summary: Christian Bear Lopez, a Queens paramedic living in Chair Lee's district, describes transporting four critically ill patients who all waited 30 minutes for ambulances, cites a $3 million FDNY EMS budget cut, and notes EMTs start at $18/hour while food delivery pays more, demanding council action on the staffing crisis.
chapters.title: Christian Bear Lopez testifies on EMS response times and budget cuts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: My name is Christian Bear Lopez, and I'm a paramedic born and raised in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Councilmember Lee, I live and work in your district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I also serve and I worship in your district of the Knights of Columbus at St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Robert Bellarmine Parish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: You chair the Finance Committee and under the fiscal 2027 preliminary plan back in July, FDNY EMS's budget was cut by $3 million and your own council report called this an EMS staffing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: This past Tuesday, I transported four critically ill patients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Two were from your district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: All four of them waited at least 30 minutes for an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: This is everyday council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Yet we call New York the greatest city in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: When NYPD, sanitation, or fire suppression needs investment, you find the money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Many of us work multiple EMS jobs just to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I know because I'm one of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: In the greatest city in the world, you can make more delivering food rather than delivering patients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: FDNY EMTs start around $18 an hour, and the people who pay the price for that underinvestment are often the most vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Older adults and disabled New Yorkers who often depend on 911 the most are on our agenda every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: When they fall, have a stroke, or cannot breathe, we are supposed to show up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: But when there is no one available to send, I have walked through that door 30 minutes, sometimes hours later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Sometimes that asthma attack is now someone dead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: And we have to stand in that family's home, look at them in the eyes, and explain why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Help took 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Not you, we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: So do not tell us that EMS is a priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I need you to prove it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: And understand this, I will be back with more EMTs and paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: When patients and their families ask why help took so long, I will tell them where these decisions are made and who represents them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I am done hiding behind the word system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Budgets are decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Staffing is a decision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Investment is a decision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: EMS may not have been on your agenda when you walked into the room this morning, and excuse my French, but after today, it better fucking be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: What are you all going to do about it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: With that, I yield my time.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Let's chat after this.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So as a representative of your district, I would love to sit and chat with you more because I think we actually share a lot of the same concerns, and so let's figure this out.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I can tell you, Council Member Chair Lee, actually working very hard internally, trying to push more funding for EMS.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We all, the people sitting here, we all understand this is the issue, and we are working on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: You approach the quieters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Next one.

chapters.summary: Michael O'Connor, a private sector EMT for eight years, describes starting wages of $20.50/hour, mandatory overtime shifts, and having to spend $60 on taxis after being mandated, earning $20 less than the additional hours paid, illustrating the affordability crisis facing EMS workers.
chapters.title: Michael O'Connor testifies on private sector EMS pay and conditions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: My name is Michael O'Connor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: I'm an EMT, and I've worked in private EMS in New York City for approximately eight years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: I want to emphasize that private EMS is distinct from the municipal sector FDNY EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: New York City's EMS workforce operates across different sectors with different employers, wages, benefits, and working conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Around approximately a few thousand or so EMS workers serve in the commercial private sector alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Today, I'm speaking from my experience as one of those private sector EMTs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: EMTs are entrusted with extraordinary responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: We perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation, provide life-saving interventions and medications within our scope of practice,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: consistently face potential exposures to infectious disease, and perform physically demanding work, including lifting and carrying patients, some of which are bariatric, which means greater than 250 pounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Yet, a starting wage of $20.50 an hour, an example of a starting private EMS rate, is still less than 21% above the New York City $17 minimum wage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: And I've even heard some stories of some private sector EMS workers getting paid less than that at $17, which is the minimum wage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Affordability affects us in very real ways, and they are interconnected with these issues that we see.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: speak today even.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: My regular schedule includes three consecutive 12-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Sometimes we are mandated past our scheduled off time because of a late job or emergency call, even when we are expected back early the following morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Recently, after one of my shifts being mandated recently, I spent about, I had to spend around $60 on taxis both ways simply to preserve enough time to sleep and return safely to care for my patients the next day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: This is around $20 more than I earned from the additional mandated hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Sometimes I feel like we are the ones paying to be mandated, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: That's only one example, though.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Affordability looks different for every EMS worker, but we should not have to choose between remaining in a profession that we love and being able to afford the basic necessity in our lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: As a New York City private sector EMT, I would feel safer knowing that the council takes seriously with allocating attention to the affordability of private sector EMS workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael O'Connor
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah, we're going to, if you guys want to stick around after this hearing, I can have a conversation with you guys.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This is more about senior free and the jury hearing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you guys want to stick around after the hearing, I can talk to you guys.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, next panel.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Wait, there are some, there are folks who still haven't spoken.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Oh, did everyone speak in this panel?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Nicholas Mosley, an FDNY EMT, describes earning $12/hour after pension deductions for 90-hour pay periods, knowing 12-year EMTs still living with parents, and single mothers working overtime plus weekend gigs just to scrape by, questioning whether he's to blame for staying in a job with insulting pay.
chapters.title: Nicholas Mosley testifies on FDNY EMT pay and living conditions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: My phone's at 1%, so I'll go quick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: My name is Nicholas Mosley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I live in Ridgewood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I'm an EMT for the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Two days ago, I had a call for a suicidal patient that had been holding for 12 whole hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: That call came in at 1 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: We arrived on scene at 1 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Throughout the day, the call was continually given to a unit, and then that unit was given a higher priority call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: For 12 hours, a person in the city suffering a mental health crisis on the verge of taking their own life was unable to receive the medical attention they deserved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Now, in my area, we were experiencing a slightly busier than normal call volume, but the simple answer as to why this person didn't get the care they needed was because we don't have enough units on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: And the simple answer as to why there aren't enough units is because our pay is insulting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: My pension dividends started getting taken out of my checks two months ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: For a 90-hour week period, I was receiving $1,050.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: $1,050 every two weeks for almost 90 hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I'll save you the effort with the math there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: That's $12 an hour I am making to respond to emergency medical calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: That number is absolutely insulting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Out of the dozens and dozens of members I know on the job, I am one of two people I know who are able to pay for their own place, who aren't living at their parents'house.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I know people who have been in EMT for 12 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: They're still living at their parents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I know mothers, single mothers who are still living with their mothers, who work 10 hours of overtime a week and then do bottle service gigs on the weekend just to scrape by living at their parents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Every single second you work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: with pay that low that forces you to struggle that much is an insult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: The fact that I'm a 26-year-old single person and I find myself working eight hours over time a week just to afford to live is an insult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I don't blame half of the people who I came out of EMS with who have already left

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: the job to be treated better somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: I don't blame the other half of the people I came out of Academy with who are only here to go to fire in five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: At this point, I worry maybe I am to blame for coming into work every day despite this insulting pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nicholas Mosley
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Omar Muhammad, a former five-year first responder, notes medical emergencies drive 70% of FDNY runs but EMS receives barely 20% of the budget, and calls on the City Council to create an independent Department of EMS with full pay parity and dedicated budget control.
chapters.title: Omar Muhammad testifies calling for independent EMS department

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Shahana Hanif, Susan Wang, and Linda Lee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: Really appreciate you guys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: You do tremendous work for the city, and thank you for giving us some of your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: My name is Omar Muhammad, and for five years, I worked as a first responder from 2017 to 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: I worked the front lines across Staten Island, South Brooklyn, throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: I experienced firsthand how our healthcare system cracked under pressure, but our first responders did not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: The raw disparity we faced on the streets mirrors institutional abandonment baked into our city budget for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: Medical emergencies now drive nearly 70% of all FDNY runs, yet barely 20% of the department budget is allocated to EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: We face the exact same biohazards, the same physical trauma, and the same life-threatening dangers unseen as fire suppression.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: But our pay and our future are treated as afterthoughts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: While top paid firefighters after five years earn roughly $110, veteran EMTs and paramedics max out at a fraction of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: Forcing thousands of experienced lifesavers to work punishing double shifts or flee the job entirely just to afford rent in the city we protect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: We carry the same weight and we deserve to be paid what we are worth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: That is why I'm calling on the City Council to create an independent Department of EMS with full pay parity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: giving us direct budget control, dedicated medical leadership, and the resources we deserve, ensuring that our city finally gets a professional emergency medical service that values the lives of its workers just as much as the lives they save.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Omar Muhammad
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Is there anyone?

chapters.summary: Alex Cardoza, a NYC paramedic, describes 6,000 daily calls becoming the norm, units sent across boroughs, 30-minute to two-hour response times, and a mass exodus from EMS, noting the recent budget increased FDNY overall but decreased the EMS division specifically.
chapters.title: Alex Cardoza testifies on EMS system failures and mass exodus

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: I guess I'll be the last one to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Alex Cardoza.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: I'm here to speak upon New York City 911, for which FDNY EMS is responsible for responding to all calls related to health emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: The FDNY has staffed approximately 60% of units for the city, allowing private agencies to supplement support for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: The average starting pay for EMTs is $18 an hour, one of, if not the lowest, of any city employee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Since 2020, the influx of calls for an ambulance has tripled to about 6,000 calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Historically, this has been known as New Year's Eve numbers, where the city has planned, staffed, and allotted personnel to account for such amount of calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Currently working as a New York City paramedic, we find that this is the norm on a daily basis with a failing system struggling to keep up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: I could sit here and tell you stories of how many calls we responded with 30-minute drive times, with terrible outcomes, but it's pointless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: The truth is you could be a unit from Queens, sent to Brooklyn, dispatched to Manhattan, or end up in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Patients and bystanders alike all say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: What took you so long?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: We waited two hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: I should have taken a cab instead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Your EMTs and medics are tired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: They're fed up and sick of being overworked and extremely underpaid compared to their first responder counterparts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Our coworkers who have been around for longer than we can imagine are telling us it's not worth it anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: It's all overshadowed by an abysmal pay scale and the stress of the traumatizing situations we are met with daily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: There's a mass exodus from EMS to anything better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: furthering the crisis we're experiencing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: The recent New York City budget has increased for the FDNY as a whole, but the EMS division has found a decrease specifically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: When you need us to come help you, the reality is you will be waiting, you will be upset, and we will be tired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: To everyone who told us to move on from a dead-end career that doesn't care about you, I say no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: City Council, you can help our first responders stay and continue to feel like it's worth it and to continue to help the city that we all imagined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: In a field where our whole point is to care for you, who cares for us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Cardoza
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Hanif acknowledges the urgency of the EMS crisis, shares frustration about the lack of dedicated hearings, and offers to meet with workers. Lee references the May executive budget hearing where EMS pay parity was discussed, notes her visit to the Bay Terrace training site, and commits to continuing the fight for EMS salary increases.
chapters.title: Hanif and Lee respond to EMS worker testimonies

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you all for joining us today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And as my colleagues shared, we recognize that this is not a problem that we're just learning about today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: This is an ongoing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And I share your frustration.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I don't have...

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: The answer nor the budget.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I share your frustration because I know that you all have been coming to hearings unrelated to the topic and you know that obviously disrupts the hearing topic.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: However, I would also love to stay behind to meet with you folks.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I don't know what your day looks like.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Obviously don't want to make that ask given you probably took time off from work to come

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: and stick around, I saw many of you here for the admin's testimony and the back and forth Q&A that we did, and you're still here.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: However, certainly this is important and the urgency couldn't be

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: couldn't be higher.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And the testimonies that you provide about the various New Yorkers, whether it be a suicide-related call, whether it be senior who needed assistance right away to folks with disabilities, this is urgent.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And you all are our first-line folks who are

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: seeing these New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: It's not us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: We are hearing about them, but it isn't us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: So I know that this isn't the time, but I do have a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And it's not, I'm not, I've asked committee staff here to check whether we have done a specific hearing on the pay parity issues.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Know that that would probably take place within the FDNY committee.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: And so not sure if this is a hearing that has taken place in that space, but would certainly be an advocate for that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But if all of you, some of you are able to stick around, and that meeting doesn't have to happen today, but

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I join my colleagues in wanting to have a further conversation so that I can get some clarity on questions that I have that have come from the testimonies you've provided today.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: But thank you all for your service every single day, for the years of service, and also for helping the next generation of frontline workers,

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: first responders, so that our city is the strongest it can be to support New Yorkers who need that care the most.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Especially be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I know we interrupted and we apologize for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I just want to let you guys know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I just want to say thank you again for letting me.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then we're going to move to the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Let's invite our Manhattan Borough President, Braham.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Pras-Homaziko.

chapters.summary: Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal thanks the council for the hearing, notes Manhattan has the largest share of SCRIE/DRIE recipients, cites average rents reaching $6,650, and urges passage of Intro 978, Council Member Cabán's resolution on automatic enrollment, and Intro 307 on universal applications.
chapters.title: Manhattan BP Hoylman-Sigal testifies supporting Intro 978 and related bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Brad Homan, Siegel Manhattan Borough President.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Really just here to thank you, Chairs Long, Hanif, and Lee, and the members of your committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
