utterances.text: You know, I represent 1.6 million Manhattanites, including the largest share of SCRI and DRI recipients in any borough of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And I'm really grateful to the council and the speaker for your hearing today, the tenants, the advocates, my state,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: former state colleagues and our city colleagues who join us in support of, in particular, Councilmember Lewis's legislation, Intro 978, as you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: From today's hearing, we're facing an affordability crisis in our rents, one which particularly impacts our most vulnerable neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: In Manhattan, rents are rising at nearly double the rate of inflation, with the average rent reaching a staggering $6,650 in August of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And we have a proven tool at our hands for seniors and people with disabilities so they don't get priced out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: The rent freeze program known as SCRI injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: But the household income limit, as again, you know, to qualify for the program has been frozen at $50,000 since 2014.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: This is tied for the longest freeze.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: in the program's history in the years since 2014, inflation in this region rose by nearly 39%,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: shelter costs over 46%, and Social Security's federally mandated cost of living adjustments reached just 38%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: This means that simply receiving inflation-adjusted Social Security could push a New Yorker above the $50,000 cap and effectively strip away their rent protections despite not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: enabling them to actually afford their rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: This has had a terrible impact on the service we are providing to a vulnerable population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And I want to thank again the council for their work, our state colleagues for authorizing the first increase in this cap in 12 years, raising that maximum income to $75,000, which represents a 50% increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I also want to thank the bills that are before you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: The one in particular that I'd like to mention, Council Member Caban's resolution to support the state bill that would raise the cap and index it to inflation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: To make also enrollment easier, Albany has to pass legislation to allow New York City to create an automatic enrollment program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Intro 307 by Council Member Marte would also ease the application process by creating a single universal application.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: HPD and the Department of Finance would jointly administer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: And just want to thank Councilmember Lewis for 978, to Senators Kavanaugh and Assemblymember Rosenthal and our other legislative partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: I'm proud to stand with you in your support and urge you to pass the bills before you today and deliver on the rent protections that our constituents deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brad Hoylman-Sigal
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the opportunity to speak to you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Board of President.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I also thank you for the work you did in Albany.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Let's see my next panel.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Alexa, und tanzing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Brenda is a Zari.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Ring, Paris, Yami.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Rabia Khalid.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Brianna McKinney.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: William Jourdain.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: When you're ready, you can begin.

chapters.summary: Lex Atham Singh of Access Justice Brooklyn supports Intro 978A, noting the $50,000 threshold hasn't been updated since 2014 while the median cost of living for two older adults exceeds $90,000, and shares stories of older adults at risk of displacement from communities they've lived in for decades.
chapters.title: Lex Atham Singh testifies for Access Justice Brooklyn

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: My name is Lex Atham Singh, and I am a Borshert Fellow in Law and Aging at Access Justice Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: I'm here today in support of the bill to increase the senior citizen rent and increase examination and jury household income eligibility threshold from $50,000 to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Access Justice Brooklyn has provided free civil legal services to the Brooklyn community for more than three decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Our service has recently expanded to include SCRIE injury enrollment and renewal assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Each year, over a quarter of our clients age 62 and older, and many rely on supplemental income to meet their expenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Government programs and benefits like SCRIE support their economic security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Current guidelines require that a household, not just an individual, make less than $50,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: These income eligibility guidelines have not been updated since 2014.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: This number does not reflect the financial reality of aging in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: The mayor's office recently reported that the median cost of living for a household with two older adults exceeds $90,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Many older New Yorkers live on a fixed income, and even those in rent-stabilized units may spend over half of their monthly income on rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: High rent costs chip away at a person's grocery budget, the money they set aside for utilities, and other expenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Increasingly older New Yorkers are unable to afford to meet their basic needs, and an unaffordable rent is a major contributor to this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: As an advocate for older adults, I often hear the phrase aging in place, referring to an older adult's ability to remain in their home and community as they age.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Many of the older adults that Access Justice Brooklyn works with have lived in their communities for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: They have strong bonds with their neighbors and often rely on community resources and members for support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Many live near the person who helps them with their finances, the person who accompanies them to doctor's visits and the supermarket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: When an older adult can no longer afford their rent, they are pushed out of the community they have long been a part of and call home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: SCRI is a vital tool to keep our neighbors in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: To maintain its vitality, it must be updated to reflect the current cost of living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: This is why I ask you to pass Bill 978A, increasing the income eligibility from $50,000 to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lex Atham Singh
utterances.text: Thank you to New York State leadership for already adopting this increase, and thank you all.

chapters.summary: Brenda Irizarry, a Bronx tenant since 1982 and member of Tenants and Neighbors and CASA, supports raising the SCRIE/DRIE income cap to $75,000, sharing that she's currently ineligible but fears future MCI rent increases in her 100-year-old building could make her unable to afford rent.
chapters.title: Brenda Irizarry testifies as Bronx tenant supporting income cap increase

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: My name is Brenda Irizarry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: I live at 3215 Bainbridge Avenue in the Bronx since 1982.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: I am a member of Tenants and Neighbors, CASA, Met Council, and Our Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: I am appealing to the City Council to increase the income cap for SCREET and DREET to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: This would benefit seniors and the disabled in several ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: More people would be eligible for these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: Also, seniors and the disabled can remain in their homes without fear of displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: It is a safety net in addition to rent stabilization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: Currently, I am not eligible for SCREED because of my income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: However, my building is over 100 years old and had two MCIs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: One resulted in a rent increase of $12 per room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: I fear that one day I won't be able to pay my rent if there are more MCIs in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: Along with other rent increases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: Therefore, I am urging the City Council to pass Intro 978A,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: raising the income limit for SCREEP and DREEP will protect our most vulnerable citizens on fixed incomes, especially in times of economic distress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brenda Irizarry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Hope we're going to pass and help everyone.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rabia Khalid of APNA Community Services, serving South Asian Muslim immigrant communities, describes how limited English proficiency, digital literacy barriers, and complex household structures compound enrollment challenges, and urges meaningful multilingual navigation support, reduced documentation burdens, and formal roles for community-based organizations.
chapters.title: Rabia Khalid testifies for APNA Community Services on enrollment barriers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: My name is Rabia, and I am the program coordinator at APNA Community Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: APNA serves South Asian Muslim immigrant, refugee, limited English proficient, older adult, and low-income communities across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Through our work in benefits navigation, case management, senior services, housing assistance, health care, food access, tax preparation, domestic violence support, and other social services, we regularly see how administrative barriers affect access to programs like screen and drink.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Eligible older adults and families can be lost on multiple points in the process from initial awareness and application to documentation, agency review, recertification, and renewals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: For the communities APNA serves, these challenges are often compounded by limited English proficiency, digital literacy barriers, cultural and ethnic backgrounds, disability, complex household structures, and unfamiliar

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Unfamiliarity with the government and systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Addressing under-enrollment requires stronger program design across the full enrollment and retention process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: First, language access should include meaningful navigation support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Translated forms are important, but many residents also need assistance understanding documentation requirements, household income rules, deficiency notices, and renewal procedures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: For many South Asian and older adults, effective access may require multilingual benefit navigation in commonly spoken languages with trained staff who can assist residents from application through recertification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Second, the city should reduce unnecessary documentation burden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: And third, recertification should be designed around continuity for eligible residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: The city should also consider the realities of multi-generational households.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Community-based organizations should also have a formal role in their enrollment systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Organizations like APNA already help residents interpret notices, and expanding this role requires dedicated funding, training, and referral protocols, and clear pathways for case escalation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Finally, the city should measure where residents are being lost in the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rabia Khalid
utterances.text: I will submit the written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Wynne Perry-Asami of Goddard Riverside, serving 22,000 New Yorkers, shares a story of a 71-year-old actress who lost income during the pandemic, fell into arrears, and was helped over five years to enroll in SCRIE, allowing her to remain in her home, and urges passage of Intros 978, 1010, and 307 with increased outreach funding.
chapters.title: Wynne Perry-Asami testifies for Goddard Riverside

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs, central and councilmatic staff, and the New York City Council for this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: My name is Wynne Perry-Asami, and I'm the Director of External Affairs at Goddard Riverside, a settlement house and social services agency serving over 22,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: A year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: One story from our Resource Center Director, Natalie Pierre-Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: An older New Yorker worked as an actress while supplementing her income through dog walking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: When the pandemic shut down performances and dramatically reduced demand for other services, her income disappeared overnight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: She quickly fell behind on rent, accumulated significant arrears, and struggled through years of uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: When she came to our program, she was not facing just one challenge, but a housing benefits and stability crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: We worked with her for five years to navigate multiple challenges, including ultimately helping her enroll in SCRI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: A, now 71, was able to remain in her home, regain a sense of security, reconnect with her community, and focus on rebuilding her home because she had that stability and that support that these programs provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: Programs like SCRI and DRI, as well as its homeowner siblings, are what make New York strong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: Intros 978, 1010, and 307, sponsored by Council Members Lewis and Marte, respectively, would expand SCRI, DRI, SHE, GD,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: eligibility, and streamline application and recertification processes, and we support swift passage and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: We support swift passage and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: We also urge, and thank you, Chair Lee, for emphasizing the importance of outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: We also urge the city to increase funding investment in outreach, enrollment assistance, and intensive case management services to support New Yorkers in need and help ensure providers and the city can continue to partner so that all of us

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: Our neighbors have trusted experience, navigation support to actually access and use these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wynne Perry-Asami
utterances.text: We'll submit full testimony.

chapters.summary: William Jourdain of Woodside on the Move, serving Queens for 50 years, supports raising the income threshold and emphasizes that expanding eligibility means little if eligible New Yorkers never enroll, sharing that his own mother benefits from Council Member Aldebol's constituent services but most seniors lack such family support.
chapters.title: William Jourdain testifies for Woodside on the Move

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: All right, well, peace and love, co-chairs, committees, excuse me, members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: I just want to say thank you for taking this time to listen to all of us here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: My name is William Jourdain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: I am the executive director for Woodside on the Move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: For 50 years, our organization has served residents across Queens, including seniors and people with disabilities struggling to remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Without a doubt, we strongly support increasing the screen injury income eligibility threshold from $50,000 to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: The current threshold simply does not reflect the financial reality of living in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Take, for example, someone earning $51,000 is not suddenly financially secure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: A senior receiving a modest Social Security cost of living adjustment or pension increase has not suddenly become wealthy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Yet that increase can affect eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: for a program designed to help that person remain in their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Raising the threshold addresses one major barrier, eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: But we also need to address another key component to this, which is participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Recent city reporting estimated more than 158,000 households

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: potentially eligible for the rent freeze program in 2023, while fewer than 68,000 households were actually receiving scree or tree benefits in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: While these figures come from different reporting years and should not be treated as a precise enrollment rate, they highlight a larger challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Expanding eligibility means little if eligible New Yorkers never successfully enroll.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: At Woodside on the Move, we see why this matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Our housing staff sit with residents trying to understand government notices

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: gather income documentation, complete applications, recertify benefits, and overcome language and technology barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Government benefits should not require someone...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Jourdain
utterances.text: Geez, all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Well, how about this?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'll give you 10 more, 15 more seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Just really quickly, Shirley, my mother happens to live in your district, so I figured I should use at least a few seconds of my testimony to let you know your office has really great constituent services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We called a few times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: But my mother has something many seniors do not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: She has someone like me who can step in when the numbers don't add up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Our public policy cannot assume everyone does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So as we consider expanding screen and DRE, our measure of success should not simply be how many New Yorkers become eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It should be how many eligible New Yorkers we actually reach, how many successfully enroll, and ultimately, how many are able to remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And one more thing that I think we should really take into consideration as we're deliberating is how we can take these consortium of bills further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We should really consider seniors being responsible for no more than a third of their monthly income on rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: These are not New Yorkers who worked here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: These are New Yorkers who worked here, raised families, paid taxes here, and helped build our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So they should be able to grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Old here, and this is what housing stability means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It means that aging with dignity and aging with respect is ultimately how we can give back to those who gave to our city for so many years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: See, Chair Lee, you did a wonderful job.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I gotta visit your mom.

chapters.summary: Brianna McKinney of Project Guardianship, providing Article 81 guardianship services, supports Intros 978A and 1010 and Resolution 431, explaining how COLA increases can push clients over the income threshold and trigger cascading benefit losses that lead to displacement into more restrictive settings.
chapters.title: Brianna McKinney testifies for Project Guardianship

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Joanne Lee and members of the Committees of Aging, Disabilities, and Finance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: My name is Brianna McKinney, and I work with Project Guardianship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: We provide guardianship services under Article 81 for New Yorkers with significant limitations and who a court has found unable to manage some or all of their own affairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: And these are people who don't have someone like you, a family member or friend, to care for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: We advocate for the least restrictive arrangement possible so that people can retain as much independence as they can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: And a big focus of ours is helping people live and age in their homes and communities despite those limitations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: We're here today to express our support for Intros 978A and 1010, which would raise the income thresholds for SCRE, DRE, SHE, and D.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: We do our work to help people stay in the community in large part by providing hands-on management of benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: Therefore, when a threshold is too rigid or a housing option doesn't exist, the consequence can mean that a client loses a rent freeze,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: behind on rent or ends up displaced into a more restrictive setting than they actually need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: For example, annual COLA increases for Social Security or Supplemental Security income can push our clients over the threshold and put a benefit that they depend on for housing stability at risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: Because our clients often rely on several benefits at once to hold their stability together, losing even one can have a ripple effect across the rest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: It's then on us as their guardian to catch that risk, reapply, or appeal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: So raising the eligibility threshold reduces the chance of potentially harmful gap in coverage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: We also support Resolution 431.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: When our clients can't find or afford housing in the community, the alternative is often a more restrictive setting than they need, which is the opposite of what Article 81 guardianship is meant to achieve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: Expanding housing options and shortening the wait for older adults and people experiencing homelessness gives guardians an actual path to keep clients in the least restrictive setting possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: We appreciate all of your work, making these benefits more accessible and effective for the New Yorkers who depend on them, and just want to say this matters not only for individual clients, but for the strength of our communities as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: When older adults and people with disabilities can remain safely and stably housed, the neighborhoods and support systems around them stay intact too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brianna McKinney
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: You have questions?

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: No, not questions, but I just wanted to thank all of you because I know a lot of your organizations and you guys do great work.

utterances.speaker: Shahana Hanif
utterances.text: I'm getting a tickle, but just wanted to say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, let's go to next panel.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Kaylin Doming, Marcus Jackson, Rebecca Paul,

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Michelle Hall.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Gracia Torres.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have a thousand.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Harlan English.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: William Ney.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Catherine Kelly.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: She's here.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, when you're ready, you can begin.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'll begin, guys.

chapters.summary: Marcus Jackson of Encore Community Services, supporting older New Yorkers for nearly 50 years, supports Intros 307 and 978A, emphasizing that housing affordability is inseparable from aging in place and urging sustained community outreach funding for older adult centers, case management programs, and trusted CBOs.
chapters.title: Marcus Jackson testifies for Encore Community Services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Zhuang, chairs and members of the Committee of Aging and Finance and Disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: My name is Marcus Jackson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Advocacy and Government Relations at Encore Community Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: For nearly 50 years, Encore has supported older New Yorkers through home-delivered meals and congregate meals, case management, benefit assistance, supportive housing, social connection, and other services that allow people to age with dignity and independence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you for holding today's hearing on SCRI injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: For the older adults, Encore serves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Housing affordability is inseparable from the ability to age in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Every additional dollar spent on rent is a dollar that may not be available for food, medication, transportation, utilities, and other necessities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Programs such as SCRI can provide critical stability, but a benefit cannot protect an older adult who does not know it exists, cannot navigate the application, struggles to produce the required documentation,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: encounters language or technology barriers, or lose assistance during the recertification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Encore, therefore, supports efforts to make those programs simpler and more accessible and easier to maintain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: We particularly support the goals of Intro 307, and we also support Intro 978-A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: These reforms recognize both the administrative

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: barriers facing applicants and the economic realities confronting older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: But legislation should be accompanied by sustained community outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Older adult centers, case management programs, housing providers, libraries, and trusted community-based organizations should be equipped and funded to help eligible New Yorkers understand these benefits, complete applications, gather documentation, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: successfully recertify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Our message today is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: New Yorkers should not lose housing stability because a benefit intended for them is too difficult to find or navigate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Encore looks forward to working with the Council, New York City Aging,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: DIFTA, of course, and our community partners to ensure older New Yorkers can access these benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Protections, their housing protections, and all the benefits that they have earned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Marcus Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, and I'll pass it over to my colleagues.

chapters.summary: Caitlin Downing of SPOP, the only agency exclusively dedicated to community-based mental health care for older adults, describes how 40% of referred clients have such dire unmet social health needs they can't participate in therapy, with housing being the most urgent need, and shares cases of suicidality and relapse triggered by housing insecurity.
chapters.title: Caitlin Downing testifies for SPOP on mental health and housing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Hi, I feel like this is celebrity sightings of all of our aging service organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Swing and other City Council Committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: I'm Caitlin Downing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: I'm the Assistant Director of Social Health at SPOP, Service Program for Older People.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: I'm grateful for this opportunity to testify in support of Resolutions 55, 470, and all legislation that improves access to stable housing for older New Yorkers, especially older adults living with mental health conditions and other disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: SPOT plays a unique role in supporting the health, emotional well-being, and independence of older adults, and we've done this for more than 45 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: We're the only agency in the city that's exclusively dedicated to community-based mental health care for older adults, and we provide individual group therapy, psychotherapy, assessments,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: medication management, psychiatric rehabilitation services to over 1,000 older adults every year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: My role at SPF is to help make sure our clients are assessed for social determinants of health, like housing, food insecurity, social isolation, and to connect people with appropriate services in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Housing, by far, is the most urgent need among the population we serve, and this need is greater every year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: About 40% of all of the adults referred to us for mental health care have such dire, unmet social health needs that they cannot participate effectively in their psychotherapy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Our goal is to address those concrete needs and stabilize our clients so they can have the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: to receive the treatment that they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Every day I hear from older adults who are at risk of losing their housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: People have expressed to me feelings of depression, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, suicidality, all around being afraid of losing their apartments, not being able to pay their rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: I meet with people who feel they've done everything right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: They get Social Security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: They might get a small pension.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: But maybe the sudden death of their partner means now their household income is cut by half.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: We have clients who are on the precipice of opiate addiction relapse because the threat of losing their home is overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Housing equals health, and programs like SCRI, DRI, and SHE are crucial to helping older adults remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Caitlin Downing
utterances.text: Thank you for this opportunity to testify today.

chapters.summary: Graciela Torres, a Bronx rent-stabilized tenant and advocate, strongly supports Intros 978A and 1010, arguing the $50,000 cap doesn't reflect NYC reality and that seniors shouldn't have to become completely poor before receiving protection from displacement.
chapters.title: Graciela Torres testifies as Bronx tenant advocate

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and members of the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: My name is Graciela Torres.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I'm a Bronx resident, a rent-stabilized tenant, and a tenant advocate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I work with seniors, people with disabilities, and tenants on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I am here today in strong support of Intro 978A and 1010, which would raise the scree and dree

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: Income eligibility cap from $50,000 to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I want to be clear, I am not here because this benefits me at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I am here because I sit with the people that this bill is meant to protect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I speak with seniors that are scared.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I speak with disabled tenants who are overwhelmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I speak with people who have lived in their homes for decades and are now afraid that New York City is slowly pushing them out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: Screen and DRE are not handouts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: They are protections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: They are what helps seniors and disabled New Yorkers stay in their home, stay in their communities, and avoid being forced into housing court shelters or homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: The current $50,000 cap does not match the reality of New York City anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: Someone can earn more than $50,000 and not be wealthy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: They can still be rent burdened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: They can still be choosing between rent, food, medications, utilities, transportations, and basic dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: I work with seniors who've saved, worked, raised families, paid taxes, and did everything they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: But now, because of the cost of living, they are being...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: treated like they make too much to qualify for help, when in reality they don't make enough to survive comfortably in this city, and that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: A senior should not have to become completely poor before the city decides they deserve protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: A disabled tenant should not have to fall into crisis before the system responds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: We should not wait until someone is in housing court facing eviction or displaced before we admit that the rules are outdated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: Raising the cap to $75,000 is not extreme, it's realistic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: It reflects what we already know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: New York City is expensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graciela Torres
utterances.text: And it is high.

chapters.summary: Rebecca Poole of the Council of New York Cooperatives and Condominiums, representing 170,000 dues-paying members, supports Intros 1010, 934, and Resolution 471, noting that increasing operating costs and Local Law 97 mandates create major affordability issues for senior and disabled co-op/condo homeowners who need help staying in their homes.
chapters.title: Rebecca Poole testifies for CNYC on co-op and condo homeowners

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs Lee, Schwang, and Hanif for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: My name is Rebecca Poole, and I'm the Director of Membership and Communication for the Council of New York Cooperatives and Condominiums, a member-funded, not-for-profit

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: organization providing information, education, and advocacy to and for co-ops and condos in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: There are over 730,000 existing co-op and condo households in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Approximately 170,000 of these are currently dues-paying CNYC members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Each co-op and condo homeowner has their own story, career, family, medical history, and economic background, regardless of their zip code.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Almost all have invested the majority of their life savings into their apartment and have committed themselves to their building community and New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: All have paid and continue to pay ever-increasing real estate taxes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Over the past 10 years, increasing operating costs and New York City mandates governing inspections, capital work, and decarbonization have created major affordability issues for cooperative and condominium

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: homeowners, particularly seniors on fixed income and disabled homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: While the Department of Finance testified that providing additional benefits to struggling homeowners would be costly, these same co-op and condo homeowners are being asked to fund Local Law 97 work they cannot afford

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: on behalf of the city without the benefits available to other LMI homeowners and landlords.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: CNYC has worked diligently on the state level to attempt to get funding specifically for these LMI homeowners, and they need help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Assistance is needed to ensure that these homeowners, many long-term New York City residents who helped build neighborhoods, can remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: The legislation proposed by Councilmember Marte will help, and CMYC is grateful for his leadership, along with that of Senator Kavanaugh and Senator Clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: CMYC strongly supports Intros 1010, 940, and Resolution 471, and urges City Council to vote in favor of those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rebecca Poole
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Michelle Hall of Rochdale Village, a Mitchell-Lama development, reports a 31.2% maintenance increase and $17.6 million unpaid water bill, urging passage of Intro 978 to help vulnerable senior and disabled cooperators facing displacement and to reduce eviction costs and empty apartments.
chapters.title: Michelle Hall testifies on Rochdale Village Mitchell-Lama increases

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: My name is Michelle Hall and I reside in Rochdale Village.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Since Rochdale Village is a Mitchell Lama development, there are cooperators who already receive SCRI and DRI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: We are under the supervision of DHCR.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: I urge all of the New York City Council members to adopt the SCRI and DRI household income increase to $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: This would enact a New York State to authorize expansion laws locally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: There are thousands of vulnerable Mitchell Lama seniors and those who are disabled cooperators that need an income increase to force SCRI and jury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Rochdale Village had a maintenance increase of 31.2%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: This is challenging increase, in my opinion, is burdensome to many cooperators who are on a fixed income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Why such a steep increase?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Rochdale Village has many unpaid bills, such as the New York City water bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: The water bill ballooned up to $17.6 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Rochdale Village also owes vendors who supposedly completed their contract assignments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Some seniors are afraid of displacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: This intro 978 would help lower the cost of eviction and empty apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: By voting yes,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: on Intro 978 would allow those seniors who were denied before because they were slightly over the $50,000 income level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: I say again, vote yes for Intro 978.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michelle Hall
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone, for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And thank you guys for supporting all the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, let's do next run.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Susan Peters.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sandra Hazel.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Milagros Petru.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Did I pronounce the name?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Melissa Reddick.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sharon Sokes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Whenever you are ready, you can begin.

chapters.summary: Sue Peters of the Upper West Side, representing the American Monetary Institute, discusses how private commercial banks create new money through lending, quoting Treasury officials from 1959, and argues this privilege is the root cause of affordability crises discussed at the hearing.
chapters.title: Sue Peters testifies on monetary reform and banking privileges

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Okay, I just want to be sure it can be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Sue Peters, and I'm a resident of the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: I am also a member of a 30-year-old 501c3 working for Monetary Reform, the American Monetary Institute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: I'm going to share an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: First, I want to say, everybody knows what this is, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This is a $5 bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: That's money, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: We don't really use that today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: We use this, our checking accounts, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This is a checking account register, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This is money, too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This money of mine in the bank, we think, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Keep that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: What I'm going to talk about addresses all the affordability crises that have been discussed in this room today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: My work experience has made me knowledgeable to share these facts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: I had a 37-year career as a data processing professional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: The last 17 years,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: I spent working for a Wall Street bank down on Wall Street, and I was responsible for their bookkeeping report, reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This is a bookkeeping, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: We don't see it, but the bank sees it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Of a corporate checking account system, had 40,000 accounts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: And move $2 trillion a day around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: So I tracked all of that with the help of some machines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: I discovered, to my total surprise, the special privilege given to private commercial banks that I worked for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Never taught to any of us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Quote, every time a bank makes a loan, all it is doing is making a bookkeeping entry in the borrower's account.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: That's all it does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This is the root cause.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: That's two minutes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can you submit a written testimony or you can wrap up in like 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Remember 2011 and the Occupy the Fed movement, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: It spread around the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: 99% fell this pressure from the 1%, the 1% of the banks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: I'm going to leave you with this quote from the Secretary of the Treasury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Of President Eisenhower in 1959.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: This is the last thing I'm going to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Quote, when a bank makes a loan, it simply adds to the borrower's deposit account in the bank by the amount of the loan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: The money is not taken from anyone else's deposit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: It was not previously paid into the bank by anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: It's new money created by the bank for the use of the borrower.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: End quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: And let me just say, the bank has that privilege in the law, but we're not told about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sue Peters
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sandra, a 68-year-old rent-stabilized tenant, describes being evicted after her aunt died, paying full rent when SCRIE benefits were cut off, being locked out of her apartment after an emergency trip to Guyana, and receiving no help despite writing to the mayor and attending rent freeze events. Zhuang offers to connect her with legal assistance.
chapters.title: Sandra shares personal eviction and landlord harassment story

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: My name is Sandra.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I'm living in a rent stabilized apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I have 20 units for the past three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I'm moving with my aunt on the 7th of July, November of 22.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: Taking care of her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: But unfortunately, she went to Guyana for an application, and she died in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I went to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: When I came back, I took the lease to DCHR because at the set time, it wasn't expired to get some guidance on what to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I was told to write the management informing him about her death, and instead of he write the lease in her name, he would renew it into my name, and I must start paying the full rent, which is $822.30 because the government was paying $477.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: 11 for her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I start paying the full rent in May of 2023.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The landlord refused to give me the lease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: He took me to court for all over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he went to his country in 2024 and he died.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The landlady for the building came from Grenada, take it over, took me back to court, and now she evicted me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I had an emergency call to Guyana in the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: And I left, before I left, on the 10th, I paid her rent for April and May.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: April, March and April.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I came back on the 23rd of June and noticed a door that she locked me out, out of my apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: And the notice said, call the landlord immediately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I did not call her because I returned about 2 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I left and I went to the friend asleep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The next morning I went to the court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The court brought my evidence, the plane ticket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The passport, my ID that I'm 68 years of age, and the judge told me that I must remove my belongings by, I think it was July of 30th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: But no luck was changed by a marshal until now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The landlord keep harassing me, telling me, come and remove my stuff out of the apartment you want to rent it.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We will follow up with you, maybe give you some legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: And I wrote the mayor on this matter on two different occasions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I posted the mail by priority mail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I went to three of his rent rip-off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: Nothing has been done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: I don't know because I talk about HRA claim that I had a heart transplant on the 4th of April 22, and I died the 9th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: The closed down HRA, the closed down the insurance.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We will get your information.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We'll follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This is an individual case.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sandra
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Milagros Franco of the Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, with 19 years of DRIE/SCRIE application experience, urges automatic enrollment, public campaigns, DOF outreach to independent living centers, and increased MOPD funding, and expresses solidarity with EMS workers on ambulance wait times.
chapters.title: Milagros Franco testifies for BCID on disability enrollment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Milagros Franco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: I'm a housing advocate at the Brooklyn Center for the Independence of the Disabled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: I have been doing dream screen applications for about 19 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: I really want you guys to approve everything you can to keep our seniors and people with disabilities in the housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: I'm just gonna read off four points.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: That I want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: As you guys have heard throughout the day, the city must centralize or coordinate the proper enrollment of tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: A lot of people don't know about screen injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: I'm always preaching about it because that's the easiest thing I can do for somebody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: The city must do an automatic enrollment for tenants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: It should be included with the HRA website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: There should be more public campaigns promoting the programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: The Department of Finance should go to the independent living centers that cater to people with disabilities and seniors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: That's where a lot of our folks come to for information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: And the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, they need more funding in order to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: to support the community-based agencies like BCID.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: And I'm right there with the fire people because I waited an hour for an ambulance when I was hurt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: So I'm right there with the fire people as well.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and attention to this urgent matter.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Milagros Franco
utterances.text: I also have the testimony, a full testimony to submit.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Melissa Reddick of the Mitchell-Lama Residence Coalition, a statewide volunteer organization, urges passage of Intro 978 to raise the income cap, citing disturbing reports of high annual increases at Mitchell-Lama developments and sharing that she personally lost benefits after a capital improvement project left her homeless for two years.
chapters.title: Melissa Reddick testifies for Mitchell-Lama Residence Coalition

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Melissa Sengret, and I serve as treasurer of the Mitchell Lama Residence Coalition, commonly known as MLRC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: Founded in 1972, MLRC is a statewide grassroot all-volunteer organization whose mission it is to work and organize for the preservation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: and future expansion of Mitchell Lama housing programs, both co-ops and rentals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: We identify, clarify, and solve common concerns of current and former Mitchell Lama residents working with elected officials and government agencies at all levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: I am also a longtime resident of Espinel Gardens, a 1,876-unit Mitchell Lama co-op located in Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: A co-op where 65% of us are on fixed income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: On behalf of the Mitchell-Lama Residence Coalition, I urge the committee to pass Intro 978, which will raise the income cap for those receiving screen-dream benefits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: In this time of burdensome inflation and ballooning housing costs, this increased income cap will allow our most vulnerable residents

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: to remain in their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: Our membership appreciates your focusing on the problems they face to pay their monthly rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: We have disturbing reports of high annual increases at many Mitchell Lama developments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: In July, the council heard about these increases

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: at its own oversight hearings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: Such increases fall heavily on our members who are disproportionately elderly and, as I said, living on fixed income.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: We want to remain in our homes, those communities we built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: Please vote to intro.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: To move intro 978 out of the committee and then support its passage by the council to protect some of our most vulnerable homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick
utterances.text: I lost my benefits because of capital improvement project that left me homeless for two years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Reddick

chapters.summary: Sharon Suggs, a 30-year Forest Hills resident and co-op owner on Social Security Disability, describes applying for the Disability Homeowners Exemption without response, rising maintenance fees and Local Law 97 burdens, and fears that increasing costs will force long-term residents, seniors, veterans, and disabled homeowners from their communities.
chapters.title: Sharon Suggs testifies as disabled homeowner on rising costs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: Hi, to distinguished members of the New York City Council Committee on Finance, thank you for giving me this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: My name is Sharon Suggs, and I'm a 30-plus year Forest Hills resident and a co-op owner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: I had to make a major transition after 25 years in the fashion industry due to my disability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: I am now on Social Security Disability, and it's very difficult to navigate resourced applications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: We have to figure out every form and program by ourselves, and it's very disheartening for both the forgotten disabled and senior citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: In the conversation, I found out about the Disability Homeowners Exemption Program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: Hence, meeting the criteria, I applied through the Public Engagement Office before the May 15th deadline, and as of today, I have heard no word.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: Over the past five years, our maintenance fees have continued to rise, especially with Local Law 97 placing an increasing burden on all of us homeowners, particularly older

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: adults and those retirees on fixed incomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: As mentioned before, Local Law 97 is approaching and the New York City local laws

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: is on the horizon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: We're deeply concerned about the added financial strain these regulations will bring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Social Security benefits and disability payments have not kept the pace with these rising costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: Personally, I'm on disability and have experienced recent medical coverage cuts, while many of my older adult neighbors are facing steep increases in their insurance premiums.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: If maintenance fees and assessments, co-op assessments continue to rise, our property tax will eventually follow suit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: This will create an unsustainable situation for long-term residents, especially seniors, veterans, and those with disabilities who may be forced

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: to leave the community that they've called home for decades with nowhere else to turn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: We respectfully ask for your support and advocacy on behalf of our vulnerable neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: It's critical that our new policies take into account the impact of those least able to absorb the additional costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sharon Suggs
utterances.text: Thank you for your attention and time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Testifying virtually, Dr. Rose of the Aging Gracefully Coalition of Faith-Based Organizations recommends expanding and streamlining all housing subsidies for seniors into a single accessible program, citing over 520 senior housing applications including 300 on HUD 202 waitlists and 220 on Housing Connect, and urging policy that addresses real economic conditions beyond poverty lines.

chapters.summary: Christian Costines of SNAP Eastern Queens Older Adult Center describes serving ethnically and economically diverse older adults in Queens, noting many low-income seniors are ineligible for SCRIE because they live in unregulated apartments or NORCs with mixed eligibility, and supports simplifying applications and raising the income threshold.

chapters.summary: Katie Bordnaro of the Mitchell-Lama Residence Coalition supports Intro 978 to raise the income cap and Intro 307 for a universal online application portal, praising the council's prior measure to auto-send SCRIE applications to Mitchell-Lama residents and urging committee passage of both bills.
chapters.title: Katie Bordnaro testifies for MLRC on Intros 978 and 307

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
utterances.text: My name is Katie Bordnaro, and I serve as Secretary of the Michelama Residence Coalition, commonly known as MLRC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
utterances.text: You heard our full description from Treasurer Millicent Reddick a few minutes ago, so I'll get right to the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
utterances.text: Today, you are hearing testimony from MLRC officers, Barbara Jones, Millicent Reddick, and myself, and members, Michelle Hall, in support of Intro

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
utterances.text: 978 to increase the income cap from $50,000 to $75,000 for those receiving scree and tree benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
utterances.text: This increase is essential to keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
utterances.text: I also want to urge you to pass Intro 307.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Katie Bordnaro
